Annotated bibliography

Kim, Dongsoo. “Lukan Pentecostal Theology of Prayer: Is Persistent Prayer Not Biblical?” <i>Asian Journal of Pentecostal Studies</i> 7, no. 2 (2004): 205–17.

Kim answers the criticism, from outside Pentecostalism, that the Korean Pentecostal stress on persistent prayer has no biblical basis. Taking the parable of the friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–8) as his test case, with the importunate widow (Luke 18:1–8) beside it, he argues that persistence is an integral part of Luke's theology of prayer, and offers this as a neglected Lukan foundation for Pentecostal theology alongside Stronstad's and Menzies's work on Spirit-empowerment. Warrington cites it as giving 'sound exegetical foundations for the importance of persistency in prayer', while warning against the slide from persistence to insistence. For the owner it is the biblical case for tarrying as sustained, effortful prayer, the Pentecostal practice the proposal sets beside Macarian ascetic striving.

How it is used in Keith Warrington, Pentecostal Theology: A Theology of Encounter, ch. 6:

  • p. 217–218 (n. 46, p. 218): Warrington cites Kim for the claim that the parables of the friend at midnight and the importunate widow 'provide sound exegetical foundations for the importance of persistency in prayer', then warns that some Pentecostals cross 'the line between persistence and insistence'.

Annotated bibliography

Hatzopoulos, Athanasios. <i>Two Outstanding Cases in Byzantine Spirituality: The Macarian Homilies and Symeon the New Theologian</i>. Analekta Vlatadon 54. Thessaloniki: Patriarchal Institute for Patristic Studies, 1991.

A study (306 pp.) of the Macarian Homilies and Symeon the New Theologian side by side, the two Byzantine writers most often accused of 'Messalian' enthusiasm because both speak of conscious, felt experience of the Spirit and of light. Edwards cites it as a work that tests Macarius' (and Symeon's) teaching against the supposed Messalian doctrines, in support of his point that the Macarian writings sometimes contradict the condemned propositions outright. For the owner it is the Orthodox answer to the first objection a Pentecostal reading of Macarius will meet (that felt Spirit-experience is Messalian), and it links Macarius to Symeon, whom Lossky also uses on the experience of grace.

How it is used in Daniel Wade Edwards, “Heavenly Fire of the Godhead” (PhD diss., Marquette, 2026):

  • p. 26 n. 103 (PDF p. 41): Edwards cites it for the claim that Macarius not only echoes but at points directly contradicts the Messalian lists (e.g. perfection is not immediately attainable even after apatheia), before his caution to 'tread gingerly'.

Annotated bibliography

Stewart, Columba. “The Ascetic Taxonomy of Antioch and Edessa at the Emergence of Monasticism.” <i>Adamantius</i> 19 (2013): 207–21.

Stewart (Saint John's Abbey) maps the kinds of ascetic in late-fourth- and fifth-century Antioch and Edessa as monasticism was forming: from Libanius and John Chrysostom in Antioch to Ephrem, Julian Saba and Rabbula's rules for clergy, the 'sons and daughters of the covenant' (bnay qyāmā) and monks in Edessa, which he calls the most detailed ascetic taxonomy in Syriac literature (repository abstract). Edwards points to it as 'a helpful breakdown of asceticism around Macarius’ lifetime'. For the owner it gives the social shape of the ascetic life Macarius addressed: ascetics living inside the Church and called simply 'Christians' rather than a separate monastic class, which matters for reading Macarian effort as ordinary Christian life (and so as comparable with Pentecostal tarrying) rather than as a monk's specialism.

How it is used in Daniel Wade Edwards, “Heavenly Fire of the Godhead” (PhD diss., Marquette, 2026):

  • p. 25 n. 99 (PDF p. 40): Edwards cites it after arguing that Macarius calls his ascetics simply 'Christians', perhaps shaped by the Syrian 'sons/daughters of the covenant', who lived celibate lives within the Church rather than as a separate community.

Annotated bibliography

Arrington, French L. <i>Christian Doctrine: A Pentecostal Perspective</i>. Vol. 2. Cleveland, TN: Pathway Press, 1993.

The second volume of a three-volume Pentecostal systematic theology by a Church of God (Cleveland, TN) New Testament scholar, published by the denomination's press; this volume covers Christ, sin and salvation. Vondey cites p. 233 for the Holiness-Pentecostal reading of the move to the altar as separation from sin and unto God, an act of Christ-like obedience through the Spirit. For the owner it is a classical Wesleyan-Pentecostal source for the altar as a practice of sanctification, the denominational 'standard' view against which Vondey's ritual reading and an Orthodox reading of tarrying can be measured.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 79: Cited (n. 100) for the ritual move to the altar as a shift of position that 'anticipates and practices separation from sin and unto God as an act of Christ-like obedience through the Holy Spirit'.

Annotated bibliography

Studebaker, Steven M. “Pentecostal Soteriology and Pneumatology.” <i>Journal of Pentecostal Theology</i> 11, no. 2 (2003): 248–70. https://doi.org/10.1177/096673690301100206.

Studebaker argues that Pentecostal soteriology, despite its experience of the Spirit, has usually subordinated pneumatology to Christology, treating the Spirit as the one who applies Christ's finished work. He proposes instead a soteriology in which the work of Christ and the work of the Spirit are integrated, engaging Kärkkäinen's interest in theosis and Macchia's pneumatological account of justification. Vondey uses it twice: for the cost of the 'second blessing' scheme (it denies the Spirit a constitutive role in justification) and for the claim that ritual sanctification is not works-righteousness. For the owner it is a Pentecostal argument, with an Orthodox (theosis) partner, for exactly the Spirit-centred account of grace that the synergy question needs.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 76: Cited (n. 82, pp. 260–65) for the point that the Pentecostal distinction between Christ's justification and the Spirit's sanctification opens the way to a 'second blessing' but 'subordinates pneumatology to Christology and denies the Spirit a constitutive function in justification'.
  • p. 79: Cited (n. 97, p. 267) for the claim that sanctification's 'performance-oriented mechanisms' do not mean Pentecostals embrace a works-righteousness theology.

Annotated bibliography

Chung, Miyon. “Conversion and Sanctification.” In <i>The Cambridge Companion to Evangelical Theology</i>, edited by Timothy Larsen and Daniel J. Treier, 109–24. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007.

Chapter 8 of the Cambridge Companion to Evangelical Theology, in its part on evangelicals and Christian doctrine. Chung treats conversion and sanctification as the Holy Spirit's work of applying Christ's atoning work: from God's side electing and transforming grace, from the human side repentance and faith that begin the Christian life. Vondey uses it for the Reformed (Calvinist) picture of sanctification as a lifelong journey of growth into grace already given. For the owner it is a standard evangelical statement of the 'already given, now lived out' view that the proposal's synergy question presses against.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 75: Cited (n. 77, 'Cf.') for the Calvinist view that 'Sanctification is learning to live out the implications of the fullness of God’s grace given to us at conversion in a journey of continual growth'.

Annotated bibliography

Yong, Amos. <i>Renewing Christian Theology: Systematics for a Global Christianity</i>. With artistic images and commentary by Jonathan A. Anderson. Waco, TX: Baylor University Press, 2014.

A one-volume systematic theology by the leading Pentecostal systematician, written for a global and renewal-shaped church, with works of art and commentary by Jonathan A. Anderson. Vondey sends the reader to its pages 103–30 for an overview of how Western traditions (Catholic, Protestant, Evangelical) relate justification and sanctification. For the owner it is a compact Pentecostal map of the Western positions that the proposal sets against Orthodox synergy, and a second Yong text beside The Spirit Poured Out on All Flesh (already in PhD 24). What Yong argues on pp. 103–30 is not checked here.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 73: Cited (n. 63) as the overview behind Vondey's claim that the dominant Western narrative identifies sanctification with justification, and so stresses 'the giving than the reception of the divine activity and grace' in the church's ritual practices.

Annotated bibliography

Burgess, Stanley M. <i>The Holy Spirit: Eastern Christian Traditions</i>. Peabody, MA: Hendrickson, 1989.

The second volume of Burgess's three-volume history of Christian pneumatology, surveying Eastern writers (Greek, Syriac, Armenian and others) on the Spirit, with sections on Pseudo-Macarius. Burgess is a Pentecostal historian, so this is the main Pentecostal scholar to read the Eastern Fathers on the Spirit before the 2000s. Richie takes from him the picture of Macarius as marked by 'a daily anticipation of the miraculous', ascetic striving for perfection, and the Spirit as 'the essential maker' of progress in grace. For the owner it is a source on how a Pentecostal reads Macarian synergy (effort with the Spirit as the maker of progress), and it belongs in the 'what has been written' part of the proposal.

How it is used in Tony Richie, Is Pentecostalism Just Another American Success Story?:

  • p. 88: Richie quotes Burgess (n. 38, p. 144): Macarius is marked by 'a daily anticipation of the miraculous' and 'a dependence on divine gifts of grace to overcome the demonic', and though the ascetic goal is 'progress in grace', 'it is the Spirit of God who is the essential maker of that progress'.

Annotated bibliography

Maloney, George A., trans. and ed. <i>Pseudo-Macarius: The Fifty Spiritual Homilies and the Great Letter</i>. Preface by Kallistos Ware. Classics of Western Spirituality. New York: Paulist Press, 1992.

The modern English translation of Collection II (the Fifty Homilies) plus the Great Letter, with Maloney's introduction (pp. 1–33) and Kallistos Ware's preface. Maloney reads Macarius as a spirituality of the heart centred on the 'personal and intimate experience of fire and baptism in the Holy Spirit', and says Evangelicals and Pentecostals will 'feel at home' with him. Ware's preface gives the three-stage progression of the heart and the balance of grace and freedom. For the owner it is the edition most Pentecostal writers (Richie among them) actually use, so it is the bridge text between Mason's 1921 translation and the Pentecostal reception; check its homily numbering against Mason before citing.

How it is used in Tony Richie, Is Pentecostalism Just Another American Success Story?:

  • p. 86: Richie cites Maloney's Introduction (n. 29, pp. 25–27) for Macarius's influence on Pietism and the Wesleys and his affinity with Pentecostal and Charismatic movements.
  • p. 86: Richie cites the Introduction (n. 30, p. 12) for the 'preponderant accent' on spiritual combat and the 'personal and intimate experience of fire and baptism in the Holy Spirit', adding that for Macarius experience serves transformation and union with God (H. 3.3, 4.15).
  • p. 87: Richie cites the Introduction (n. 36, p. 27) for Maloney's claim that Evangelicals and Pentecostals will 'feel at home' with Macarius because of 'openness to the Holy Spirit and the personal experience of God's grace'.

Annotated bibliography

Turner, Victor. <i>The Anthropology of Performance</i>. New York: PAJ Publications, 1987.

A posthumous collection of Victor Turner's late essays (preface by Richard Schechner) on ritual, social drama, carnival and 'performing ethnography'. It extends his earlier work on rites of passage, liminality and communitas into a theory of performance: ritual as a sequence of enacted, culturally shaped practices that do not merely express but bring about change in the people who perform them. For the owner it is the anthropological source behind Vondey's reading of sanctification as ritual performance, and so behind the claim that altar practices (tarrying, coming forward) are transformative rather than merely symbolic. Read it with Alexander's Turnerian article on Pentecostal possession (already in Encounter Research, 9TCU386F).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel:

  • p. 79: Vondey cites Turner (n. 96, p. 75) for speaking of sanctification as ritual, 'the performance of a sequence of practices determined by cultural, ecclesial, and doctrinal processes', before arguing this is not works-righteousness but a rite of passage with ontological status.

The AG's doctrine of sanctification is clearly synergistic. With respect to the AG's distinctions between positional and progressive sanctification, it is more synergistic regarding the latter than the former. That is, whereas God will not save a man without his faith and assent, he absolutely cannot transform him without his continued faith and assent.⁶⁸ One is first positionally sanctified in Christ (at conversion), but one needs to experientially appropriate sanctification in a life-long process of growth. In this regard, the Holy Spirit and faith are not only necessary for salvation, they are necessary for the whole of the Christian experience. Put another way, a believer, by faith and the Holy Spirit, may be […]

p. 259

[…] was unquestionably the drawing work of the Spirit. The same holds true for the Christian's sanctification; once drawn into Christ, the Spirit will consistently and lovingly prompt and call the believer toward Christ-likeness.

p. 260–61

[…] or the language about hypostasis and ousia. Nonetheless, Pentecostals do know that when they experience the Spirit's presence, they are experiencing the person of God himself; this in contradistinction to the Reformed and Wesleyans who describe God's working in the less personal terminology of grace: prevenient or common or universal, and saving or regenerating or special. Strangely resembling the Orthodox' own synergistic model, though expressed within its own respective theological-contextual milieu, the Pentecostals' anthropology is inextricably tied together with its pneumatology. Human beings were created for fellowship with God, and that in the most intimate of ways - between persons.

Ch. "Sanctification's Theological Foundations" (photographed by the owner).

p. 243

Although the moment of justification is described by the AG primarily in juridical terms, as the above has clarified, it is not understood solely therein. Upon one's salvation one is simultaneously adopted into God's family (Jn 1:12,13; Rom. 8:15,16; 1 Jn. 3:1). Because of Christ's atoning work, those who […]

p. 247

[…] sanctification, but that we progress in sanctification."²⁶ Whereas Christ is the basis for the believer's sanctification, and provides the righteousness by which the believer is continually being transformed, the Holy Spirit is the person of the Trinity who draws the believer to - and makes the believer become like - Christ in the process of progressive sanctification. Jesus' role in effecting believers' positional sanctification was completed when he died on the cross. But the Spirit continues to apply the benefits of Christ's cleansing blood.²⁷ Pearlman said, "He makes real in believers what Christ has done for them." The Spirit has not come to take Christ's place, instead he has come to "make Christ real."²⁸

p. 250

In its teaching about progressive sanctification the AG rightly can be called synergistic. A person can do nothing to save himself (conviction of sin and repentance are themselves works of the Holy Spirit),⁴² but he must cooperate with the workings of the Holy Spirit, and obey the Holy Spirit, if he is to increasingly become like Christ. It is the believer's responsibility to yield his or her bodily members unto the Lord's righteousness. This yielding is accomplished via an act of faith, an assent of the heart to God that Christ's work on Calvary is accepted as payment for sin. Addressing the question of whether a person has anything to do in one's sanctification other than accepting God's plan in faith, an official AG publication answered, "No and yes. He merely accepts, but that acceptance involves a fight of faith." That fight of faith involves walking by faith with the Spirit and refusing to allow himself to yield to sin.⁴³

p. 250

Whereas a person knows he or she is justified and has been granted positional sanctification based upon one's salvation experience, the person can know he or she is progressing in sanctification based on the fruit of the Spirit that is being produced within. These Christian virtues (love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control; Gal. 5:22-3), or marks of Christian character, cannot be produced by one's self-effort, or by one's own ascetic attempts to subdue one's body and/or sinful impulses. Instead they result from one's yieldedness to God, faith, and cooperation with the Holy Spirit's leading.⁴⁴ It should also be clarified, the AG has long taught that one's spiritual giftings (the charismata of 1 Cor. 12:8-10) do not necessarily make one more spiritual or more sanctified.⁴⁵ The same can be said regarding spiritual experiences.⁴⁶

Bird, Michael F. “Progressive Reformed Response.” In *Justification: Five Views*, edited by James K. Beilby and Paul Rhodes Eddy. London: SPCK, 2012. (US edition: Downers Grove, IL: IVP Academic, 2011.)

Bird's short reply, from his 'progressive Reformed' position, to Kärkkäinen's 'Deification View' in the IVP/SPCK multiview volume on justification (with Horton, Dunn and O'Collins). Black quotes it for one charge: Kärkkäinen 'nowhere ... defines what he actually means by theosis or deification', when ideas of theosis range from 'absorption of the divine nature' to 'conformity to the image of Christ'. For the owner it is the sharpest Protestant objection to a Pentecostal theosis, and a check on how any proposal using deification language defines it. It sits beside Kärkkäinen's own chapter in the same book, which Black cites at pp. 223–24 ('participation in God, the presence of Christ in the believer through the Holy Spirit, or theosis').

How it is used in Black, The Church in the Eternal Purpose of the Triune God:

  • p. 192, n. 1211: Black quotes Bird (p. 250) to open his question 'what exactly does Kärkkäinen mean by theosis?', then tests Kärkkäinen's and Mannermaa's definitions and finds them imprecise (pp. 192–93).

Annotated bibliography

Isaac of Nineveh. *Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh: Translated from Bedjan's Syriac Text with an Introduction and Registers*. Translated by A. J. Wensinck. Verhandelingen der Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen te Amsterdam, Afdeeling Letterkunde, Nieuwe Reeks 23, no. 1. Amsterdam: Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen, 1923.

The first English translation of the ascetical homilies of Isaac the Syrian (Isaac of Nineveh, 7th c.), made by the Dutch orientalist A. J. Wensinck from Paul Bedjan's Syriac edition (Paris, 1909). Lossky says he refers 'mainly to Wensinck and sometimes to the Theotoki Edition' (the Greek translation, ed. N. Theotokis, Leipzig, 1770; p. 200, n. 1), and Isaac is his chief witness for the whole middle of ch. 10: the three stages of penitence, purification and perfection, repentance without end, the gift of tears, and prayer rising into silence and ecstasy. The passage you marked (p. 208, n. 3) is Isaac on the saints who 'no longer pray, their minds having been engulfed in the Divine Spirit', which Lossky uses for the 'spiritual silence which is above prayer'. For your direction it is the Syriac ascetic voice behind Lossky's picture of encounter as silence and rest rather than ecstasy, the point your note on p. 208 sets against 'shouting in tongues'. A newer English version exists (The Ascetical Homilies of Saint Isaac the Syrian, Holy Transfiguration Monastery, 1984; rev. 2011) but its page numbers differ (not checked against Wensinck here).

How it is used in Lossky, The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church, ch. 10 'The Way of Union':

  • p. 208 (PDF p. 13), n. 3: 'Theotoki ed., XXXII, p. 202; Wensinck, p. 115': Isaac's saying that 'as the saints in the world to come no longer pray ... so the mind, when it has been made worthy of perceiving the blessedness of the age to come, will forget itself' (your purple) grounds Lossky's 'spiritual silence which is above prayer'.
  • p. 200, 204–8 (not marked orange): Isaac is cited throughout: n. 1 p. 200 (the edition note), the three stages and repentance (p. 204), the movements of the soul partaking of the Spirit and 'his very liberty is taken away' (pp. 207–8).

Callahan's volume (xxiii + 288 pp.) is the standard English translation of Gregory's ascetic treatises, including *On the Christian Mode of Life* (*De instituto christiano*, from p. 125), *On Virginity*, *On Perfection*, the *Life of Macrina* (p. 161) and *On the Soul and the Resurrection*. *De instituto christiano* is the treatise Lossky quotes on grace and free will as "two poles of one and the same reality". The authorship question matters for you: Werner Jaeger (1954) argued that Macarius' *Great Letter* depended on this treatise, but since Reinhold Staats the consensus runs the other way. *De instituto* is Gregory's reworking of the Macarian *Great Letter*. So Lossky's Cappadocian proof text for synergy probably has Macarius behind it. That links your two lenses, the Cappadocians and Macarius, at the very point of synergy. My writing: 2026-11-09 (Lossky, "The Way of Union")

11.9.26 - Lossky and Deification - The Way of Union (Chapter 10)

Wow, what a stellar reading. All the questions I have had on deification are being summed up here. There is a lot in this writing, only a few pages in.

There is no doubt that the Eastern view of the Christian life is one of "continual effort" toward the goal of "attaining the Spirit." I love the aim of the Orthodox life is gaining the Spirit. And as it seems, this is not just a once and done thing, as if you are striving to receive one moment of love from the Spirit, but a continual grasping and receiving of the Holy Spirit. This is the aim.

This is where it gets weird. This pursuit of the Spirit, a language I love that fits into Eastern asceticism, is a "constant effort of will". There is a co-operation of our will (found in the heart) and God's grace. It is a synergy of the two. They are not two separate chapters in a systematic theology, they somehow rely on each other. In my opinion, this makes human will on the same par of God's grace.

God has created the objective path of grace, which goes out to all humanity, and we must respond in our own subjective walking of the path. As Lossky says,

"If God has given us in the Church all the objective conditions, all the means that we need for the attainment of this end, we, on our side, must produce the necessary subjective conditions: for it is in this synergy, in this co-operation of man with God, that the union is fulfilled. This subjective aspect of our union with God constitutes the way of union which is the Christian life." (196).

There is a mystery here whereby "grace and human freedom are manifested simultaneously and cannot be conceived apart from each other." (197).

This is an anti-thesis to St. Augustine who describes God's grace sometimes over our free will (I think). Lossky at least says that St. Augistine fell into the same pitfall Palegius did when trying to talk about these two thigns separately 'grace' and 'free will'. There are not two separate subjects, but somehow a bueaitiluf cop-operation.

I wonder if the incarnation or the Spirit's mingling with our spirits may help shine some light on this. The human and divine in perfect harmony. For the Spirit's role is to bring us to Jesus, and to reveal Jesus. Jesus who is the God-man.

How does this relate to Pnl (Pentecostalism)?

There is inherent in Pnls are call to tarry and seek the Lord. To dance and sing and cry out for the Spirit to come (Maranatha is a key phrase in Pnl worship). We call our and seek Him and trust that He will respond. We often pray until an answer is given.

We trust Jesus' words, "If you seek me, you will find me." We seek until we find.

This is why the altar has become a central spiritual practice of Pnl worship. It is the 'yes and amen'! to what Jesus is calling us to. He has cleared the path through the woods in his life, death, burial and resurrection, and now it is up to us to throw our hands up, to run to the altar, and place our face into the grace of Jesus.

There is a very real holiness aspect of this as well. We strive for holiness, much in our Wesleyan roots. As Stephanie Gretzinger often says, "The closer you draw, the less you can take with you." This holiness is often a battle of our will (where Lossky places in the heart.) as St. Macarius describers, and Lossky points toward: the heart is 'a workshop of justice and injustice'.1 It is a vessel which contains all the vices, but where at the same time, God, the angels, life and the Kingdom, light and the apostles, and the treasures of grace are to be found'. (Lossky 201).

We must be vigilant in our pusruit of Jesus. For this is always the goal. We do not pursue holiness, we pursue Jesus who is altogether holy and a consuming fire.

Finally, there is an element of outward mission that the Holy Spirit leads us toward. I am intrested to see if Lossky points in this direction.

Of course, Pnls would describe the working of God's grace as the Baptism of the Holy Spirit, or encounters with Jesus. This is where Macarius can help here. For he describes an active involvement of the Holy Spirit and a pursuit of Him until He encounters us.

Macarius then can give support for encounters with the Spirit, a tarrying for the Lord, a deification of the soul as we tarry, and a communal aspect of salvation.

'The ascent to deification is accomplished not through noetic contemplation but through surrender to divine love, by which humans become christs', and deification is 'attainable here and now' (abstract). Virtue acquired and surrender together is the exact tension in the owner's 'is tarrying synergy or petition?' question (report 19). It is also the strongest Byzantine analogue to Pentecostal experiential claims.

📖 Read this

Whole article, with Coulter's response, pp. 165–77 (Coulter 178–200)

The only Orthodox–Pentecostal exchange on holiness/sanctification.

Annotated bibliography

Kazarian, Nicolas. "Discernment of Holiness and Holy Persons." Journal of Pentecostal Theology 33, no. 2 (2024): 165–77. https://doi.org/10.1163/17455251-33020002.

The Orthodox paper in the Orthodox–Pentecostal Academic Dialogue pair on holiness, published with Dale Coulter's 'Holiness in Pentecostal Discourse' (JPT 33.2, 178–200; report 15). Report 15 listed only Coulter's half. This is the one place where the official dialogue sets Orthodox holiness (saints, discernment) beside Pentecostal sanctification. It is therefore the live test of 'partner or foil' between the owner's two traditions [content not read; title and pagination from Crossref].

📖 Read this

Whole chapter, pp. 568–85

An hour's overview of theosis as divine–human communion by the author of the ascesis line.

Annotated bibliography

Papanikolaou, Aristotle. "Theosis." In The Oxford Handbook of Mystical Theology, edited by Edward Howells and Mark A. McIntosh, 568–85. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198722380.013.29.

A compact overview by the leading American Orthodox theologian of theosis and practice. It addresses the 'red flags' theosis raises for some Christians and roots the doctrine in Christology ('who do you say that I am?'). Papanikolaou's wider work (Being with God, 2006, in Zotero as GCTQQM2L; The Mystical as Political, 2012) treats ascesis and virtue as the form of divine–human communion. This essay is the quickest way into that line. It is the same Handbook as the Dysinger 'Asceticism' chapter already used in report 17 [editor Mark A. McIntosh's middle initial from standard citation].

📖 Read this

Whole chapter, pp. 522–44

An Orthodox self-critique of the 'foil' rhetoric; explains the Greek books you just added.

Annotated bibliography

Kalaitzidis, Pantelis. "Contemporary Greek Orthodox Theologians." In The Oxford Handbook of Deification, edited by Paul L. Gavrilyuk, Andrew Hofer, and Matthew Levering, 522–44. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2024. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198865179.013.49.

Kalaitzidis covers theosis in Mantzaridis, Nellas, Romanides, Yannaras, Zizioulas, Loudovikos, Papanikolaou and others from the 1960s onward. He traces how the 'return to the Fathers' and the Athonite revival made theosis 'an Orthodox identity marker and an integral part of Orthodox anti-Westernism' (abstract). For the owner, it gives the context of four items in the new Zotero collection (Mantzaridis, Nellas, Yannaras, Zizioulas; and Vlachos in the Romanides line). It also shows when deification is set up as a foil to Western sanctification for identity reasons rather than on theological grounds.

📖 Read this

Macarius section of the chapter, pp. 123–36

Your primary author, in the 2024 standard reference, by a supervisor lead.

Annotated bibliography

Plested, Marcus. "Deification in Macarius, Evagrius, and Dionysius." In The Oxford Handbook of Deification, edited by Paul L. Gavrilyuk, Andrew Hofer, and Matthew Levering, 123–36. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2024. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198865179.013.10.

Already in Zotero (3MVUANYG). Plested judges that of the three, 'Macarius provides the richest and most robust teaching on deification', with 'striking imagery of divine fire and light, and sound advice born of his own spiritual experience' (abstract). It is the shortest current scholarly bridge from Orthodox deification to the owner's Macarius–tarrying project. It is also the place to check how Plested handles Macarian synergy (EM 3.1; Hom. 26) against charges of Messalianism.

📖 Read this

The soteriology chapter and the concluding evaluation, pp. UNVERIFIED (370–78 pp.; contents not available online)

Where the evangelical critique of Stăniloae's synergy is made.

Annotated bibliography

Bartoș, Emil. Deification in Eastern Orthodox Theology: An Evaluation and Critique of the Theology of Dumitru Stăniloae. Paternoster Biblical and Theological Monographs. Carlisle: Paternoster, 1999.

A Romanian Baptist's doctoral study (supervised by Kallistos Ware and Oliver Davies; foreword by Ware), reissued by Wipf & Stock in 2007. It works through Stăniloae's apophaticism, anthropology, Christology, soteriology and ecclesiology as organised by deification. It then evaluates them from an evangelical standpoint, which includes the role of human cooperation and the sacraments in salvation [the synergy focus of the critique is general knowledge; the contents were not seen]. It is the fullest evangelical 'foil' reading of Orthodox synergy, written with Orthodox sympathy, and useful because Pentecostals stand close to its evangelical concerns. See also Bartoș, 'The Dynamics of Deification in the Theology of Dumitru Stăniloae', in Dumitru Stăniloae: Tradition and Modernity in Theology, ed. Lucian Turcescu (Iași: Center for Romanian Studies, 2002).

📖 Read this

The anthropology section (deification, person and freedom), pp. UNVERIFIED (the whole study is pp. 1–130)

The most up-to-date map of where human freedom and participation sit in modern Orthodox debate.

Annotated bibliography

Maican, Petre. Deification and Modern Orthodox Theology: Introduction to Contemporary Debates. Brill Research Perspectives in Theology. Leiden: Brill, 2023. https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004547100.

A 130-page critical survey (Brill Research Perspectives) that tests the claim, going back to Popov, Lot-Borodine and Lossky, that deification is the 'pillar' of modern Orthodox theology. Maican examines anthropology, Trinity, tradition/epistemology and ecclesiology. He finds deification central to anthropology and Trinity, much weaker in ecclesiology, and used 'implicitly' to justify readings of tradition (p. 108, per a review). It is the best recent map of the debates (Zizioulas vs Loudovikos on person and freedom, sophiology) in which synergy sits. A reviewer suggests modern Orthodox identity rests less on deification than on claiming a distinct experience of God, which matters for the 'foil' question (review summary; book not read).

📖 Read this

Ch. 4, 'Repentance in the Treatises of St Mark the Monk', pp. 88–117 (verified via Crossref); optional ch. 1, 'True and False Repenting', 9–35

Mark the Monk is the Greek Father who most directly discusses grace, works and effort; ch. 1 shows how Reformation categories shaped the scholarship.

Annotated bibliography

Torrance, Alexis. Repentance in Late Antiquity: Eastern Asceticism and the Framing of the Christian Life c.400–650 CE. Oxford Theology and Religion Monographs. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013.

Torrance shows that in Mark the Monk, Barsanuphius and John, and John Climacus, repentance is not a single penitential act but the frame of the whole Christian life. His opening chapter reviews the study of repentance 'from the Reformation to the present'. Mark the Monk, who wrote 'On those who think they are justified by works', holds together the gift of baptismal grace and the need for lifelong struggle. For the owner this is the patristic material behind the question 'how much participation?': effort as the appropriation of grace already given, not as merit. It works as a bridge between the traditions on works and grace. [Subtitle, series and ISBN verified in library catalogues (MPDL, CAS); chapter pages via Crossref.]

📖 Read this

Whole article, pp. 271–80

Ten pages; ascesis as embodied deification, the 'practice' answer to how much we participate.

Annotated bibliography

Hamalis, Perry T., and Aristotle Papanikolaou. "Toward a Godly Mode of Being: Virtue as Embodied Deification." Studies in Christian Ethics 26, no. 3 (2013): 271–80. https://doi.org/10.1177/0953946813484405.

A short Orthodox virtue-ethics essay: human flourishing is 'the progressive realization of theosis—a godly mode of being cultivated through liturgy and askesis, marked by the embodiment of the full range of virtues, and crowned by a radical love' (abstract). It is the clearest recent statement of human participation as practice (askesis, habituation, embodiment). That links Orthodox synergy to the owner's 'transformation of body and soul' thread and to Western virtue traditions, as a partner in method though not in the theology of grace.

📖 Read this

Whole article, pp. 934–58

Explains where the East/West 'foil' binary came from, and why it turns on whether the human person takes part.

Annotated bibliography

McInroy, Mark. "How Deification Became Eastern: German Idealism, Liberal Protestantism, and the Modern Misconstruction of the Doctrine." Modern Theology 37, no. 4 (2021): 934–58. https://doi.org/10.1111/moth.12700.

McInroy argues that the modern picture of deification as 'an exclusively Eastern Christian doctrine antithetical to Western theology' comes from F. C. Baur. Baur read the Fathers through German Idealism as teaching 'an automatic, mechanical deification of humanity as a whole that leaves the individual no role to play in his or her salvation', and Ritschl then excluded it from Western theology (abstract). This bears directly on the owner's question: the 'foil' story rests on a version of deification without synergy. The Fathers' deification does involve the person's participation, which reopens partnership with Western sanctification. McInroy is a possible supervisor (Oxford). See also his 'Before Deification Became Eastern: Newman's Ecumenical Retrieval', IJST 20, no. 2 (2018): 253–68.

📖 Read this

§§4–7, pp. pp. 1–3 of the PDF (numbered paragraphs)

Twenty minutes; the agreed definitions, in both traditions' words.

Annotated bibliography

Lutheran–Orthodox Joint Commission. "Salvation: Grace, Justification and Synergy." Statement of the Ninth Plenary, Sigtuna, Sweden, 1998. https://ecumenical-institute.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/1998-Lutheran_Orthodox_Dialogue-EN.pdf.

A three-page official dialogue statement, read in full. It defines Orthodox synergy as 'working together' of divine grace and the human will 'in the appropriation of the divine life in Christ', grounded in the Christological point that Christ's human will 'was not abolished' (§5). Both sides affirm 'the absolute priority of divine grace' and that grace is not 'irresistible'. Lutherans 'do not use the concept of synergy' but 'recognize the personal responsibility of the human being… in the growth of faith' (§5). Both affirm 'real participation by grace in the nature of God' (§6), and the Orthodox locate 'the struggle against passions… in the power of the Holy Spirit' as participation in Christ's death and resurrection (§7). It is the clearest official map of where synergy partners and where it divides from sola fide sanctification.

📖 Read this

Whole chapter, pp. 620–34

Exactly the owner's question; recent (2024).

Annotated bibliography

Despotis, Athanasios. "Deification, Justification, and Sanctification." In The Oxford Handbook of Deification, edited by Paul L. Gavrilyuk, Andrew Hofer, and Matthew Levering, 620–34. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2024. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198865179.013.38.

An Orthodox New Testament scholar (systematic section of the Handbook) on the three categories the owner is comparing. According to the abstract, early Christian deification means 'moral assimilation and ontic participation in God' as a way of life. 'The idea of justification by πίστις does not challenge synergism in this progress but defines who belongs to the people of God'. Justification and sanctification are 'aspects of an ongoing theomorphic transformation of baptized believers'. This is the most recent explicit treatment of synergy alongside justification, and it argues for partnership, not opposition (content from the OUP abstract; chapter not read).

📖 Read this

Whole article, pp. 647–59

One hour; names synergy as the dividing line between patristic deification and Reformation participation.

Annotated bibliography

Gavrilyuk, Paul L. "The Retrieval of Deification: How a Once-Despised Archaism Became an Ecumenical Desideratum." Modern Theology 25, no. 4 (2009): 647–59. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-0025.2009.01558.x.

The leading critic of loose 'theosis' talk. Gavrilyuk surveys the discovery of deification in Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, Edwards and the Wesleys and finds 'little agreement on what is constitutive of deification', which makes it 'an ecumenist's dream and a philosopher's nightmare'. His key claim for the owner: the Greek patristic doctrine 'includes synergistic anthropology and sacramental realism that are in tension with the Reformation understandings of participation in God' (abstract). Synergy is therefore what marks Orthodox deification off from Protestant sanctification. It is a foil, unless the Western partner is Wesleyan or Catholic. Gavrilyuk is also on the owner's supervisor list (Oxford).

data.note:
📖 Read this

The opening part on the 'health' of primordial human nature and the general principles of therapy (grace and human cooperation), pp. UNVERIFIED (volume and page structure of the English edition not confirmed)

Where the cooperative principle is set out before the catalogue of passions.

Annotated bibliography

Larchet, Jean-Claude. Therapy of Spiritual Illnesses: An Introduction to the Ascetic Tradition of the Orthodox Church. Translated by Kilian Sprecher. Montreal: Alexander Press, 2012.

A scholarly synthesis of the Fathers' 'therapeutics' (from the 4th French edition): the original health of human nature, the passions as illnesses, and the virtues and ascetic means as their cure, culminating in deification. Larchet presents healing as grace and human cooperation together, with heavy use of Maximus. His work on Maximus (La divinisation de l'homme selon saint Maxime le Confesseur, Cerf 1996; 'The Mode of Deification' in the Oxford Handbook of Maximus, 2015) is where his account of synergy is most precise. The book can be read as a partner to holiness-tradition sanctification (healing the heart) [general knowledge; not read this session].

📖 Read this

The opening chapter(s) defining 'Orthodox psychotherapy' and the illness and cure of the nous, pp. UNVERIFIED

States the therapeutic model of synergy in its strongest, most polemical form.

Annotated bibliography

Hierotheos (Vlachos), Metropolitan of Nafpaktos. Orthodox Psychotherapy: The Science of the Fathers. Translated by Esther Williams. Levadia: Birth of the Theotokos Monastery, 1994.

A popular, influential account (in the line of John Romanides) of Orthodox theology as therapy: the purification of the nous through ascesis and hesychastic prayer, leading to illumination and theosis. Human effort is unambiguously required, as a patient's cooperation with the physician. The book is sharply anti-Western and treats Augustinian and scholastic theology as the loss of this therapeutic method. It is a strong 'foil' voice, useful as evidence of the polemical strand that report 17 calls a heuristic of emphasis, not of essence [general knowledge; not read this session].

📖 Read this

Chapters 'Man' and 'The Church', pp. UNVERIFIED (chapter titles from the Logos listing)

Freedom, sin and participation, set out briefly and with the anti-Western edge.

Annotated bibliography

Yannaras, Christos. Elements of Faith: An Introduction to Orthodox Theology. Translated by Keith Schram. Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1991.

A short catechism (xiv + 167 pp.) of Orthodox doctrine. Its chapters run from knowledge and the problem of God through Trinity, World, Man and Jesus Christ to the Church (chapter list per Logos). Yannaras frames salvation as the person's free entry into the Church's communion and ethos, and he sets this pointedly against Western 'individual' moralism and legal categories. That makes it a clear example of the 'foil' reading the owner should weigh against more irenic voices (Louth, Despotis) [general knowledge of Yannaras; this book not read this session].

📖 Read this

Ch. 1, 'Personhood and Being' (esp. the closing section on ecclesial hypostasis), pp. UNVERIFIED (about pp. 27–65, from memory)

The core statement of freedom and participation as communion; the foil to an individual effort model.

Annotated bibliography

Zizioulas, John D. Being as Communion: Studies in Personhood and the Church. Contemporary Greek Theologians 4. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1985.

Zizioulas places deification in ecclesial and eucharistic personhood. The person passes from 'biological' to 'ecclesial' existence through baptism and Eucharist, and freedom means being constituted by communion. For the synergy question this is an alternative to ascetic effort: participation is ecclesial and sacramental before it is moral. Torrance (2020, ch. 1) and others criticise this personalism as weak on ascesis and on Christ's humanity, and report 17 has already noted the 'eucharistic versus ascetic' tension. DUPLICATE of UZ7D9C6W.

📖 Read this

The chapters on the Holy Spirit and on prayer (titled 'God as Spirit' and 'God as Prayer' in standard printings), pp. UNVERIFIED (chapter titles from memory)

Where Ware treats the Spirit's work and the human response in prayer, the nearest to tarrying.

Annotated bibliography

Ware, Kallistos. The Orthodox Way. Rev. ed. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1995.

Ware's introduction to Orthodox faith as a way of life, organised around God (mystery, Trinity, creator, man, spirit, prayer, eternity). It presents deification as a journey in which grace and freedom work together and in which prayer and ascesis are the human share. It is irenic, a partner text. For a more explicit synergy passage, Ware's The Orthodox Church (ch. 'God and Man') and his 'Salvation and Theosis in Orthodox Theology' (1983; see report 19) are better [general knowledge; chapter titles not checked this session].

📖 Read this

The later chapters on deification through the sacraments and through prayer/hesychasm and the moral life, pp. UNVERIFIED (137 pp.)

Where Palamite theosis becomes concrete practice: the human side of participation.

Annotated bibliography

Mantzaridis, Georgios I. The Deification of Man: St Gregory Palamas and the Orthodox Tradition. Translated by Liadain Sherrard. Contemporary Greek Theologians 2. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1984.

A compact study (137 pp.) of Palamas's teaching: deification as participation in the uncreated energies, received through the sacraments and appropriated through prayer, ascesis and the keeping of the commandments. For the owner it shows how the essence–energies distinction lets Orthodox writers say both that deification is wholly God's gift (uncreated grace) and that it requires human cooperation. That is the 'grace is not a created habit' contrast already noted in report 19 [general knowledge; text not read this session].

📖 Read this

The chapter on Cabasilas and justification/redemption within deification (Part Two); otherwise Part One on the image, pp. UNVERIFIED (254 pp.)

Directly about whether Western justification categories can sit inside Eastern deification.

Annotated bibliography

Nellas, Panayiotis. Deification in Christ: Orthodox Perspectives on the Nature of the Human Person. Translated by Norman Russell. Contemporary Greek Theologians 5. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1987.

Nellas grounds deification in an anthropology of the image: the human being is created 'in' Christ the archetype and is dynamically oriented toward him, so human growth is the realisation of what the person already is. The book draws heavily on Nicholas Cabasilas. Nellas reads Cabasilas's language of justification as integrated into, not opposed to, deification [general knowledge; chapter title UNVERIFIED]. That makes it one of the clearest Orthodox 'partner' readings of justification and sanctification. Kalaitzidis's Handbook chapter places Nellas within the Greek debate.

📖 Read this

Introduction (on the goal of Orthodox spirituality and the roles of grace and freedom) and the opening chapters of Part One, 'Purification', pp. UNVERIFIED (397 pp.; the section titles could not be seen online)

Where Stăniloae sets out the principle of cooperation before applying it to the passions and virtues.

Annotated bibliography

Stăniloae, Dumitru. Orthodox Spirituality: A Practical Guide for the Faithful and a Definitive Manual for the Scholar. Translated by Archimandrite Jerome (Newville) and Otilia Kloos. South Canaan, PA: St Tikhon's Seminary Press, 2002.

A full Orthodox ascetical theology in the Philokalic scheme: purification, illumination, perfection. Its stated goal is 'the deification of man and his union with God, without being merged with Him' (publisher description). Stăniloae treats every stage as the joint work of grace and free effort, and the virtues as both gift and achievement. This is the strongest systematic form of Orthodox synergy and the main target of Bartoș's evangelical critique (see new-sources). It reads as a partner to Wesleyan and holiness sanctification rather than a foil [general knowledge; text not read this session].

📖 Read this

Ch. 2, 'Perpetual progress or eternal rest?' (or, for one hour, the Conclusion), pp. 40–81 (ch. 2); 197–216 (Conclusion): verified via Crossref

Ch. 2 asks whether deification is endless human striving or rest in Christ's perfected humanity, which is the 'how much participation' question in patristic form.

Annotated bibliography

Torrance, Alexis. Human Perfection in Byzantine Theology: Attaining the Fullness of Christ. Changing Paradigms in Historical and Systematic Theology. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020.

Through Maximus, Theodore the Studite, Symeon the New Theologian and Palamas, Torrance argues that human perfection is defined by Christ's own humanity: 'what is true of Christ's humanity becomes true of the humanity of the saints by grace' (OUP abstract, ch. 2). He challenges the popular Orthodox idea of endless striving (epektasis) as the shorthand for theosis and stresses rest and stasis in Christ. This makes the book a Christocentric check on effort-heavy readings of synergy, close to the owner's own question about what Christ has already done and what remains for us to do. It is also the most substantial recent Orthodox monograph on the theme (reviews in JTS 2023, SJT 2022, Nova et Vetera 2023, The Thomist 2022).

📖 Read this

Athanasios Despotis, 'Deification, Justification, and Sanctification' (ch. 38); then Pantelis Kalaitzidis, 'Contemporary Greek Orthodox Theologians', pp. 620–34 (Despotis); 522–44 (Kalaitzidis): verified via Crossref

Despotis addresses the owner's exact question (synergism and justification/sanctification); Kalaitzidis shows where the 'foil' rhetoric comes from. Plested's Macarius chapter (123–36) is already in Zotero as 3MVUANYG.

Annotated bibliography

Gavrilyuk, Paul L., Andrew Hofer, and Matthew Levering, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Deification. Oxford Handbooks. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2024.

The current reference work (44 chapters, 2024), and the volume for 2015–2026 work on the owner's question. Athanasios Despotis's chapter argues that in early Christianity 'the idea of justification by πίστις does not challenge synergism' in the process of transformation. He treats justification and sanctification as 'aspects of an ongoing theomorphic transformation' (OUP abstract), which makes them partners, not foils. Pantelis Kalaitzidis shows how theosis became 'an Orthodox identity marker and an integral part of Orthodox anti-Westernism' in Greek theology, which is the foil reading the owner should be able to recognise. There is no Pentecostal chapter; Castelo covers Pietism, the Moravians and the Wesleys (371–85).

📖 Read this

The whole essay, pp. 32–44 (range partly verified; cited pp. 33–41 confirmed by other scholars). Also in Louth, Selected Essays II (OUP 2023), 178–90

One hour; the best short statement of why deification, and with it human participation, frames everything in Orthodoxy.

Annotated bibliography

Louth, Andrew. "The Place of Theosis in Orthodox Theology." In Partakers of the Divine Nature: The History and Development of Deification in the Christian Traditions, edited by Michael J. Christensen and Jeffery A. Wittung, 32–44. Grand Rapids, MI: Baker Academic, 2008. First published Madison, NJ: Fairleigh Dickinson University Press, 2007.

Louth argues that deification is not one doctrine among others but 'structural' for Orthodox theology: it sets the pattern of the whole 'mosaic'. It forms a larger arch from creation to deification, within which the smaller arch from fall to redemption sits (pp. 33–35, as cited by Leidenhag). He also notes that deification fell out of the centre of Western theology from about the twelfth century. For the owner, the essay explains why Orthodox writers treat human participation as the goal of creation and not only as a consequence of forgiveness, and this is where the 'partner or foil' question bites. Louth is conciliatory, not polemical, so the essay reads as a partner text.

📖 Read this

Chapters 'Self-transcendence' and 'Participation in the divine life' (plus the epilogue 'Do you live it?'), pp. UNVERIFIED (chapter titles verified in the Library of Congress contents note; the book is 189 pp.)

The two chapters where the human side of theosis (ascesis, sacraments, prayer) is treated; the closest thing to a 'synergy chapter' in the book.

Annotated bibliography

Russell, Norman. Fellow Workers with God: Orthodox Thinking on Theosis. Foundations Series 5. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2009.

Russell's short, pastoral companion to his 2004 OUP monograph. The title comes from 1 Cor 3:9 (synergoi, 'fellow workers'), so the whole book is framed around divine–human cooperation. The chapter sequence (economy of salvation, image and likeness, transfiguration, self-transcendence, participation, union) moves from God's initiative to human appropriation, and it ends with an epilogue that asks 'Do you live it?'. It is a likely partner text for the owner: it presents theosis as the Orthodox counterpart of sanctification, not its rival [general knowledge; the book was not read this session].

data.note:
Annotated bibliography

Polkinghorne, John. Reason and Reality: The Relationship between Science and Theology. London: SPCK, 1991.

A short (119-page) book by the Cambridge mathematical physicist turned Anglican priest, setting out his 'critical realism' and arguing that science and theology are both truth-seeking disciplines about one reality. Kärkkäinen's n. 324 cites p. 103, where (as Kärkkäinen reports it) Polkinghorne grants that the Orthodox may be right that deification is 'the destiny of creation'. That fits Polkinghorne's wider eschatology: creation is destined to share in God's life, and the new creation is what the Spirit does with the old one, not a replacement. For the owner it is a lead for the later body–matter chapter: deification read as the Spirit's transformation of matter, not only of souls. Same-year US edition: Philadelphia: Trinity Press International, 1991 (ISBN 1-56338-019-6). Which edition Kärkkäinen used is not stated in the chapter.

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC p. 275 (PDF p. 30); n. 324 on EC p. 288 (PDF p. 43): Kärkkäinen cites the 'Anglican physicist-priest' Polkinghorne as agreeing that deification is 'the destiny of creation', to argue that the Eastern doctrine can speak to science, ecology and creation.

Annotated bibliography

Peacocke, Arthur. Theology for a Scientific Age: Being and Becoming—Natural, Divine, and Human. Enl. ed. Theology and the Sciences. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1993.

Peacocke's Gifford Lectures, the major statement by the biochemist-priest of a theology fitted to an evolving cosmos (God as continuous creator acting in and through natural processes; panentheism). In the same orange highlight as Polkinghorne, Kärkkäinen cites p. 430 n. 22, where Peacocke says deification is probably 'more congenial to an evolutionary perspective than the traditional, often Western, language of redemption, salvation, sanctification, etc.' The page number points to the enlarged 1993 edition (the 1990 Blackwell first edition is far shorter). For the owner this is a second science-and-theology voice to pair with Polkinghorne in a later Spirit-and-matter chapter: on this view theosis is the frame that suits a world of growth and becoming. Peacocke is a liberal panentheist, so he is a conversation partner, not an ally on bodily encounter.

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC p. 275 (PDF p. 30); n. 325 on EC p. 288 (PDF p. 43): A second 'scientist-priest' supporting the claim that deification language suits an evolutionary, creation-wide account of salvation better than Western forensic terms.

Annotated bibliography

Lossky, Vladimir. The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church. Translated by members of the Fellowship of St. Alban and St. Sergius. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1976. First published London: James Clarke, 1957.

The classic twentieth-century Orthodox synthesis (French original 1944), which shaped how Western readers see theosis: apophatic theology, the essence–energies distinction, and the separate 'economy' of the Holy Spirit. Kärkkäinen's n. 57 points to pp. 196–99, which (as far as we know, unchecked) open ch. 10, 'The Way of Union'. That chapter treats union with God as synergy, the free cooperation of human will with grace, and Kärkkäinen also cites ch. 10 for union in n. 36. He uses it for the line the owner marked purple: grace is 'a presence of God within us that demands constant effort on our part'. For the owner, this is the Orthodox text behind Kärkkäinen's synergy, and the place to test his own pursuit/tarrying thread (findings §2b-7) against an Orthodox account of effort inside grace. Findings §2 already notes that Lossky's Spirit chapter is ch. 8.

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC pp. 250–51 (PDF pp. 5–6); n. 57 on EC p. 280 (PDF p. 35): Supports the claim that in the East grace and freedom are never set against each other: 'It is not a question of merit but of cooperation, a synergy. Grace is a presence of God within us that demands constant effort on our part.'
  • p. EC p. 249 (PDF p. 4); nn. 36, 41 (also n. 56, p. 174): Cited elsewhere in the same section for union with God (ch. 10) and for theosis being 'echoed by the fathers and the theologians of every age'.

data.note:
Annotated bibliography

Pannenberg, Wolfhart. Systematic Theology. Vol. 1. Translated by Geoffrey W. Bromiley. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 1991.

The first volume of Pannenberg's three-volume dogmatics (German 1988): the truth of Christian doctrine, the concept of God, revelation, the Trinity and the divine attributes. In the treatment of God's attributes he defines God's holiness through the 'true infinite' (after Descartes and Hegel): the infinite both separates itself from the finite and includes it, so God's holiness 'enters the profane world, penetrates it, and makes it holy'. Kärkkäinen builds his 'trinitarian-driven account of holiness' on this, against a withdrawal-from-the-world holiness. For the owner it gives a metaphysical reason why holiness can be 'contagious' and reach bodies and things, which links to the body–matter chapter and to the Spirit-as-field debate already in findings §1 (ST vol. 2).

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC p. 272 (PDF p. 27); n. 298: Source of the quotation 'enters the profane world, penetrates it, and makes it holy' (ST 1:400), the green you highlighted; n. 297 (ST 1:399) gives the infinity argument just before it.

Annotated bibliography

Runyon, Theodore. The New Creation: John Wesley's Theology Today. Nashville: Abingdon Press, 1998.

A standard reading of Wesley by the Candler (Emory) systematic theologian. Runyon organizes Wesley's theology around the renewal of the image of God and the 'new creation' of persons, society and the cosmos, and closes by bringing Wesley into present questions (human rights, women, the poor, the environment). Wesley here is a theologian of real change, not only of pardon, and Runyon is one of the Methodist writers who place him near the Eastern Fathers. Kärkkäinen uses him twice: for Wesley's view that the new birth begins a life that must grow, and for Wesley's socially directed holiness. For the owner it is the Wesleyan link in the chain Macarius → Wesley → Holiness → Pentecostal (findings §2b-11; Wesley sermon on the calendar Wed Nov 11).

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC p. 272 (PDF p. 27); n. 292: Runyon pp. 71-74: Wesley presents 'a similar view' to Moltmann's, that the life born anew 'wants to grow'.
  • p. EC p. 273 (PDF p. 28); n. 303: 'For a fine detailed discussion' (Runyon ch. 6) of 'Wesley's deeply socially oriented holiness spirituality' as 'a positive example of the deep link with earthly realities'.

Annotated bibliography

Moltmann, Jürgen. The Spirit of Life: A Universal Affirmation. Translated by Margaret Kohl. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1992.

Moltmann's pneumatology (German original Der Geist des Lebens, 1991), the fourth of his 'contributions to systematic theology'. Part One grounds the doctrine of the Spirit in experiences of the Spirit in everyday life as well as in Scripture and tradition; Part Two follows the Spirit through the order of salvation (liberation, justification, regeneration, sanctification, charismatic powers). Kärkkäinen leans on it for every step of his account of holiness as growth: life 'born anew' from the Spirit 'wants to grow' (p. 161), the Spirit as the power of growth (p. 162), sin as sickness and the Eastern/Wesleyan balance (p. 164), sanctification as the sanctity of life and creation (pp. 171, 175). For the owner it is the main Protestant source behind the sentence the owner marked with the effort question (EC p. 272), and a Western ally for experience of the Spirit as the place where justification and growth happen.

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC p. 272 (PDF p. 27); n. 292: Quoted for 'Every life that is born wants to grow ... The life we say has been "born again" ... also wants ... to arrive at its proper form' (Spirit of Life p. 161), right after 'Christian life is not static'.
  • p. EC p. 272 (PDF p. 27); n. 293: 'So also' (p. 162) for the claim that 'although human effort is called forth, ultimately growth ... is the matter of the power of life, the divine Spirit', the sentence of your effort question.
  • p. EC p. 272 (PDF p. 27); n. 294: 'For comments' (p. 164) on the Eastern Church and Wesleyan movements finding balance more easily, with sin 'not so much as a transgression to be atoned as a sickness to be healed'.
  • p. EC pp. 271-73; nn. 290-91, 296, 301-2, 304: Also cited, unhighlighted, for sanctification as 'the inevitable consequence of justification' (p. 164), holiness (pp. 171, 174-75) and Methodist social holiness (pp. 165-66); and earlier for justification 'through this experience of the Spirit' (p. 146, nn. 209-10, EC p. 264).

data.note:
Annotated bibliography (from Black, thesis p. 193)

An essay in a collection of seventeen of Kärkkäinen's own essays, edited by Amos Yong, arguing that Pentecostal-Holiness theology should take up theosis. It gives three reasons (as Black reports them): deification is 'an ecumenically fruitful and biblically-theologically legitimate image of salvation' with 'some roots' in Pentecostal-Holiness tradition; it is 'a pneumatologically rich concept' that corrects soteriologies built on Latin christology and 'forensic-juridical' categories; and encounter with the East clarifies 'free will and synergia' (pp. 162–65). It also offers Mannermaa's 'leaven' definition (pp. 151–52) and suggests a Mannermaa-style 'finding' of theosis in Pentecostal-Holiness texts (p. 162). For the owner it is the primary text behind Black's critique and the place to test whether a Pentecostal theosis must be synergistic, which bears on human participation and tarrying (§2b-7).

p. 193: n. 1214 (the orange highlight): p. 149, Kärkkäinen's phrase 'a human being becoming a god', which Black says does not mean pantheism or an ontological change of humanity into divinity.

p. 192: nn. 1209–10, 1212: p. 150 (he admits the Mannermaa school is controversial), p. 162 ('perhaps a similar kind of finding could happen when Pentecostal-Holiness texts are searched'), pp. 151–52 (Mannermaa's 'leaven' definition, the p. 192 purple).

p. 193–94: nn. 1215–23: pp. 162–65, the three reasons for Pentecostals to explore theosis, ending with 'free will and synergia' (p. 164), which Black then tests against the Apostolics' monergism (pp. 195–97).

p. 191: n. 1203: listed first among Kärkkäinen's attempts to appropriate theosis for Pentecostal theology.

Ramelli's translation of the unexpurgated Syriac Kephalaia Gnostika, with commentary. It is the text behind Tsui's KG references on the mind's 'nakedness', its becoming 'like light', and the body as the soul's organon and 'chariot' (KG 1.67). Ramelli also wrote Ch. 3 of this volume, on Origen's influence on Nyssa.   • p. 113–114: n. 17, the body as organon of the soul (KG 1.67 and others; pink), with Ramelli 2015 cited for the 'instrumental body'.

Sinkewicz, Robert E., trans. *Evagrius of Pontus: The Greek Ascetic Corpus*. Oxford Early Christian Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003. https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199259939.001.0001.

The standard English translation of Evagrius's Greek ascetic works: Praktikos, Chapters on Prayer, On Thoughts, To Eulogios, Foundations, Eight Thoughts and others. Tsui quotes from it throughout, including every Evagrius passage you marked pink (Chapters on Prayer 128 and 142; On Thoughts 16; Praktikos 15, 29, 52). For your project it is the primary text to read for Evagrian ascesis, moderation and fasting.

How it is used in Tsui, “The Body in the Ascetic Thought of Evagrius Ponticus”:

  • p. 112: Source of the translations of Ch. Pr. 128 and On Thoughts 16 (pink, n. 12).
  • p. 114: Ch. Pr. 142, 'hold always to your citizenship in heaven' (pink reference).
  • p. 120–121: Praktikos 15, 29 and 40 on moderate ascesis and the body's health (green and pink).

Annotated bibliography

Konstantinovsky, Julia. *Evagrius Ponticus: The Making of a Gnostic*. Farnham: Ashgate, 2009.

Konstantinovsky, an Orthodox scholar at Oxford, gives a full account of Evagrius's ascetic and contemplative system, including the path from praktikē through natural contemplation to knowledge of the Trinity, and the place of the body in it. Tsui relies on it for Evagrius's tripartite anthropology and for the goodness of the body. For your project it is a standard guide to Evagrius, the Father you will need as a foil to Macarius (Plested's 'functionally pantheistic' Evagrius, findings §2b-15).

How it is used in Tsui, “The Body in the Ascetic Thought of Evagrius Ponticus”:

  • p. 110: Cited at n. 7 (pp. 29–31) for the progress from vice to praktikē and the stages of contemplation (a sentence you marked pink).
  • p. 118: Cited at n. 34 (p. 122) for the ascetic body as the 'ideal instrument' of the soul. You marked the reference in pink.

Annotated bibliography

Hunt, Hannah. *Clothed in the Body: Asceticism, the Body and the Spiritual in the Late Antique Era*. Farnham: Ashgate, 2012.

Hunt studies how late-antique ascetic writers, including Syriac ones, held the physical and the spiritual together. She takes the image of being 'clothed' in the body as her organising motif and argues that what the ascetics opposed was 'fleshly behaviour rather than actual corporeality'. It appears twice in this volume: in Tsui on Evagrius, and in Kaldas (Ch. 8, p. 181 n. 67) for the Syrian roots of Macarius's clothing imagery. For your project it is a bridge text on the body in ascesis and on Macarius's garments of light (the body's share in glory).

How it is used in Tsui, “The Body in the Ascetic Thought of Evagrius Ponticus”:

  • p. 118: Cited at n. 33 (p. 51): Evagrius's 'flesh' echoes Paul's 'living according to the flesh'; the problem is fleshly behaviour, not having a body. You marked the reference in pink.
  • p. 181: Kaldas (Ch. 8, n. 67, not annotated) cites the Routledge 2016 printing, pp. 137–157, 'on the Syrian roots of the clothing motif' in Macarius.

Annotated bibliography

Tobon, Monica. “Raising Body and Soul to the Order of the Nous: Anthropology and Contemplation in Evagrius.” In *Studia Patristica 57: Papers Presented at the Sixteenth International Conference on Patristic Studies Held in Oxford 2011*, vol. 5, *Evagrius Ponticus on Contemplation*, edited by Markus Vinzent, 51–74. Leuven: Peeters, 2013. https://doi.org/10.2307/jj.35841818.7.

Tobon explains Evagrius's anthropology (mind, soul and body as dimensions of the fallen nous) and how contemplation raises body and soul to the order of the mind (Great Letter 22). Tsui uses it to set out the 'Platonic tripartition' you wanted to understand 'as a basis' (your note, p. 110). For your project it gives the clearest account of the Evagrian alternative to Macarian and Cappadocian bodily transformation: the body is raised, but into mind.

How it is used in Tsui, “The Body in the Ascetic Thought of Evagrius Ponticus”:

  • p. 110: Cited at n. 5 (p. 53), with Cartwright, for the fallen mind having soul and body as its differentiated dimensions. You marked the reference in pink beside your 'I need to understand what this means as a basis' note.

Annotated bibliography

Zachhuber, Johannes. *Human Nature in Gregory of Nyssa: Philosophical Background and Theological Significance*. Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae 46. Leiden: Brill, 2000. https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004274327.

The standard monograph on Nyssa's concept of the universal human nature (physis) and its philosophical sources, with its role in Trinitarian theology, Christology and soteriology. Gregory's view that Christ assumes and transforms the whole of human nature is central to it. For your project it is the scholarly anchor for 'whole humanity, body and soul together' (Vigorelli p. 108) and for any claim that deification in Nyssa concerns the human race as a whole and not just individual souls.

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 83: Cited at n. 15 (pp. 154–162), with Brugarolas, for the holistic anthropology implied by the doctrine of creation. You marked it in pink.

Annotated bibliography

Brugarolas, Miguel. “Divine Simplicity and Creation of Man: Gregory of Nyssa on the Distinction between the Uncreated and the Created.” *American Catholic Philosophical Quarterly* 91, no. 1 (2017): 29–51. https://doi.org/10.5840/acpq2016127102.

Brugarolas examines how Nyssa's doctrine of divine simplicity and his created/uncreated distinction shape his account of the creation of the human being. Vigorelli cites it as evidence for the 'holistic effect in anthropology' that the Christian doctrine of creation introduced, as an alternative to a Platonic body–soul opposition. For your project it supports the claim that the body is part of the image, and it also guards the creature/Creator line that deification language must keep.

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 83: Cited at n. 15 with Zachhuber for creation doctrine as a holistic alternative to Platonic body–soul dualism. You marked the reference in pink.

Annotated bibliography

Karfíková, Lenka. “The Metaphor of the Mirror in Platonic Tradition and Gregory’s Homilies on the Song of Songs.” In *Gregory of Nyssa: In Canticum Canticorum; Analytical and Supporting Studies*, edited by Giulio Maspero, Miguel Brugarolas, and Ilaria Vigorelli, 265–87. Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae 150. Leiden: Brill, 2018. https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004382046_013.

Karfíková traces the mirror metaphor from Plato and the Platonists into Nyssa's Homilies on the Song of Songs, showing what Gregory takes over and what he changes. It pairs with Hart 2002 as the philological side of the same theme. For your project it can show whether Nyssa's 'transformation by gazing' is a Platonic inheritance or something new, a question that also runs through Kaldas on Macarius (Ch. 8).

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 101: Cited at n. 101 together with Hart on the soul as connatural with the divine. You marked it in pink.

Annotated bibliography

Hart, David Bentley. “The Mirror of the Infinite: Gregory of Nyssa on the *Vestigia Trinitatis*.” *Modern Theology* 18, no. 4 (2002): 541–61. https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0025.00203.

Hart reads Nyssa's image of the soul as a mirror of the infinite God and argues that, for Gregory, the human person reflects the Trinity in an endlessly dynamic way, an analogy of the Trinity in the person rather than in static faculties. For your project it is the key secondary text on the 'mirror' passage you marked (the soul 'receives the likeness of what it freely chooses to gaze on', pp. 91–92), and on transformation as an ever-increasing reflection. It may help with your coin image ('we continually shine the coin', outline).

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 101: Cited at n. 101 on the soul as 'connatural (syngenes) with what is divine' (Nyssa, hom. in Cant. 11). You marked the reference in pink.

Annotated bibliography

Maspero, Giulio. “The Fire, the Kingdom and the Glory: The Creator Spirit and the Intra-Trinitarian Processions in the *Adversus Macedonianos* of Gregory of Nyssa.” In *Gregory of Nyssa: The Minor Treatises on Trinitarian Theology and Apollinarism*, edited by Volker Henning Drecoll and Margitta Berghaus, 229–76. Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae 106. Leiden: Brill, 2011. https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004194144_012.

A study of Nyssa's treatise on the Holy Spirit against the Pneumatomachians, centred on its images of the Spirit as fire, kingdom and glory and on the Spirit's role as Creator within the Trinitarian processions. Of the sources in this volume, it is the closest to your question 'what about the Spirit?' (your note, p. 98). Nyssa's 'fire' and 'glory' language for the Spirit is also a possible bridge to Macarius's 'fire and Spirit' texts (findings §2b-14) and to Pentecostal fire imagery.

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 100: Cited at n. 99 together with Thomas 2019 on the fourth-century turn in pneumatology. You highlighted the footnote marker in pink.

Annotated bibliography

Thomas, Gabrielle. *The Image of God in the Theology of Gregory of Nazianzus*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2019. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108593410.

A monograph on the image of God across Nazianzen's orations and poems, covering creation, the fall, the image's restoration in Christ and its growth in the life of the Church. Vigorelli cites pp. 127–133 on the turning point in pneumatology between the third and fourth centuries. For your project it is a direct way into the Cappadocian (Nazianzen) side of image, Spirit and transformation, and it may be useful beside Or. 31 and 41 (findings §3, Nazianzen never read with repeated encounter).

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 100: Cited at n. 99 (pp. 127–133) on 'the historical-dogmatic turning point in pneumatology' between the 3rd and 4th centuries. You marked the footnote marker in pink beside Vigorelli's account of the Spirit as the being 'given and received and given back'.

Annotated bibliography

Maspero, Giulio. “Patristic Trinitarian Ontology.” In *Rethinking Trinitarian Theology: Disputed Questions and Contemporary Issues in Trinitarian Theology*, edited by Robert J. Woźniak and Giulio Maspero, 211–29. London: T&T Clark, 2012.

Maspero, a leading Nyssa scholar at the Pontifical University of the Holy Cross, argues that the Cappadocians, and Nyssa above all, moved relation from an accident to the inner life of God, an 'ontology' of relation. Vigorelli builds her chapter on this thesis. It matters for your project because it gives a Cappadocian, Trinitarian reason why deification is relational (participation as relationship) rather than substance-change, which is one route into 'encounter' language.

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 100: Cited at n. 97 for relation as 'the constitutive immanence—the inner life—of the divine nature' in Nyssa's distinction of the three hypostases.

Some details unverified, see sources.json.

Annotated bibliography

Vigorelli, Ilaria. “Ontology and Existence: Schésis of the Soul in Gregory of Nyssa’s *In Canticum Canticorum*.” In *Gregory of Nyssa: In Canticum Canticorum; Analytical and Supporting Studies*, edited by Giulio Maspero, Miguel Brugarolas, and Ilaria Vigorelli, 527–38. Supplements to Vigiliae Christianae 150. Leiden: Brill, 2018. https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004382046_030.

Vigorelli's own earlier study of schesis (relation, disposition) of the soul in Nyssa's Homilies on the Song of Songs, which is the technical basis for the relational anthropology of her chapter in this volume. It treats the soul's inner disposition toward the good as an ontological condition that is conformed to what it loves. It bears on your direction as a patristic grammar of transformation by relationship and encounter, read through the Song of Songs, which Nyssa uses for epektasis. You have Norris's translation of the Homilies in your library (HKR7GZUA).

How it is used in Vigorelli, “Gregory of Nyssa’s Trinitarian Anthropology”:

  • p. 99: Cited at n. 96 for the claim that Gregory's distinctive idea of relation (schesis) in anthropology comes from his Trinitarian dispute with Eunomius. You marked both the footnote and its marker in pink.
  • p. 104: Cited again (n. 113, 'Vigorelli, 2018') for the 'inner… spiritual (free and voluntary) relation with the beloved'.

Summary: Tsui argues that Evagrius's view of the body is 'unified and integrated with soul and mind' (abstract, p. 109), against the picture of desert asceticism as hatred of the body (p. 109). Within an Origenist, Platonic tripartition, the fallen mind has soul and body as 'its differentiated dimensions' (p. 110). Its ascent reunites them: practical ascesis (praktikē) leads to apatheia and then to stages of contemplation, until 'the body will be elevated to the rank of the soul, the soul to that of the mind' (GL 22; pp. 110–11). The problem is not the body but 'flesh', the body dominated by passions. Anachoresis, the 'flight from the body', means detaching the soul from the sensory world, not rejecting the body (pp. 113, 121). The body is God's good creation and the 'instrument' (organon) of the soul. Disciplined, it becomes 'a chariot for the rational soul' and 'a vehicle for salvation' (pp. 117–19), and Evagrius warns against extreme ascetic measures, which come from demons, so that ascesis keeps the body healthy (pp. 120–21).

Your highlights and notes (Preview), with a summary

Summary: Vigorelli reads Gregory of Nyssa's anthropology as a coherent 'narrative', in the sense of an akolouthia or ordered sequence (p. 78, note *), shaped by Gen 1:26–28, by the Trinitarian dispute with Eunomius, and by Christology against Apollinaris. Her main claim is that concupiscence depends on sin and not on the body. The passions are a departure from an original, natural desire for the good (physikē schesis pros to agathon), and that desire involves 'the unity of soul and body' and 'will be preserved in the eschatological state' (pp. 78, 96). The 'tunics of skin' stand for mortality, not for the body itself (pp. 95–96), and death is a God-given 'medicine' and 'therapy' that frees the body–soul unity for the resurrection (pp. 97–98). Gregory's Trinitarian idea of relation (schesis) then gives a picture of the soul as a mirror conformed to what it gazes on (pp. 91–92, 101). In that picture desire is not abolished in union with God; it becomes love that never reaches satiety, which is epektasis that 'does not exclude the body' (pp. 101–5). She concludes that the Incarnation 'transformed the logic of participation in the divine into a personal relationship that does not exclude the body, but rather assumes it' (p. 107), through 'the union of the Word with all humanity, body and soul together' (p. 108).
