Your highlights and notes (Preview), with a summary

Summary: The editors' Introduction (pp. vii–xiv) presents the volume as the outcome of the workshop 'Bodily Resurrection vs Immortality' at the 2019 Oxford Patristics Conference, and states its aim: to explore 'the diversity of individual lived experiences and theoretical approaches to the unity of body and soul' in authors of the second to seventh centuries (p. vii). It then summarises each of the twelve chapters in turn (pp. viii–xiii). Its recurring claim is that the Fathers balanced 'a dualist lexicon' with 'holistic anthropological and Christological statements' (p. xi). It closes with the aims of the new series (pp. xiii–xiv).

Annotated bibliography

Macchia, Frank D. “Tongues as a Sign: Towards a Sacramental Understanding of Pentecostal Experience.” <i>Pneuma</i> 15, no. 1 (1993): 61–76. https://doi.org/10.1163/157007493X00059.

Macchia's well-known proposal that speaking in tongues can be understood as a sacramental sign: an outward, bodily sign of the Spirit's presence and action rather than only a piece of evidence for a doctrine. It is the main source behind Castelo's sentence that tongues made the Pentecostal self 'sacramental' and that God 'sacramentalized' the body (p. 50). For the owner it is the closest Pentecostal text to the margin note on p. 50 (tongues as the body, voice and lungs taken up into heavenly language), and so a bridge from tongues to the body changed in encounter (compare Palamas, Triads II.ii.13, healing and tongues working 'through the body', findings §2). Reprinted in the Brill volume Pentecostal Ecclesiology (2016), pp. 125–43.

How it is used in Daniel Castelo, Tarrying on the Lord:

  • p. 50: n. 71: cited for tongues as 'an external, bodily sign of the inward presence and activity of the Spirit', right before the orange-marked line that 'all holdouts' resistant to God 'were publicly defied in a moment in which God ‘sacramentalized’ one’s body'.

Annotated bibliography

Saliers, Don E. “Liturgy and Ethics: Some New Beginnings.” <i>Journal of Religious Ethics</i> 7, no. 2 (1979): 173–89.

Saliers, a Methodist liturgical theologian, argues that the relation between liturgy and ethics is best put by showing how particular affections and virtues are formed and expressed in communal prayer and ritual action, and he ties worship to an ethics of character. It is the article Castelo's essay sets out from and corrects: Castelo says Saliers treats affections and virtues as if they were the same thing (p. 32). The same journal issue carries responses by Paul Ramsey, Margaret Farley and William Everett. For the owner it is a source for the claim behind the altar, that worship forms the worshipper ('How we pray and worship is linked to how we live'), and so for encounter as formation rather than a one-off feeling.

How it is used in Daniel Castelo, Tarrying on the Lord:

  • p. 49: n. 68: quoted for 'How we pray and worship is linked to how we live—to our desires, emotions, attitudes, beliefs, and actions', which opens Castelo's section on tarrying; the owner noted 'How we pray is how we live. That is good.'
  • p. 31–32: nn. 1–2, 4: the opening thesis (affections and virtues formed in communal prayer) and the 'internal, conceptual link between liturgy and ethics', which Castelo then criticises for running the two frameworks together.

Annotated bibliography

Crews, Mickey. <i>The Church of God: A Social History</i>. Knoxville: University of Tennessee Press, 1990.

A social history of the Church of God (Cleveland, TN), the Holiness-Pentecostal denomination in which Castelo is ordained. Castelo cites its pp. 108–37 for the denomination's early pacifism, when members 'suffered persecution (and at least one suffered death)' for refusing military service, and for how far that conviction later shifted. For the owner it is historical evidence for Castelo's claim that Pentecostal identity was once carried by concrete, costly holiness practices, which bears on the owner's question 'Where does our P identity come from?' (p. 34). It is background, not a theological source on encounter or deification.

How it is used in Daniel Castelo, Tarrying on the Lord:

  • p. 48: In n. 63, as the example of a 'more pronounced shift' than in the Assemblies of God: the Church of God moved from persecuted pacifism to leaving war to 'individual conscience', which Castelo calls conformity to Enlightenment individualism.

11.8.26 - Catello - Tarrying on the Lord

Castello begins by defining the problem on Pnl spirituality, that it is based in the affections that often change. He then moves into Aristotelian and Aquinas ethics to create a system whereby the Spirit must enliven the affections (encounter) that are then sustained by Christian habits (tarrying).

I have not thought much about Pn; identity, although I probably should begin. it seems that Castello is addressing a modernizing of Pentecostalism whereby we have shucked off our holiness husks to become more relevant to the world, while still maintaining activity of the Spirit. This seems a separate essay, but perhaps dear to Castello's heart as he describes ethics. I have not finished it yet, but it has been a thrilling read so far.

It also makes me excited in PhD to study those the fathers studies, such as Plato and Aristotle, and to see, as Clement of Alexandria said, the "vestiges of the Trinity" in those great philosophers. I wonder in what ways Macarius was influenced by these philosophers, in regards to theology, and in regards to this essay, virtue.

He has not spoken about tongues as a marker of other Pnl experiences, for it reads that he still desires particular ethical modes to be markers of Pn identity, namely holiness practices. I wonder if he will get into these things. Will he posit a Footloos town as a new Pnl stronghold?

data.title: Tarrying on the Lord: Affections, Virtues and Theological Ethics in Pentecostal Perspective
data.abstractNote: As Pentecostals begin to inquire what might constitute Pentecostal theology, the matter must also arise as to what constitutes Pentecostal ethics, both as a matter of logical sequence and as a necessity given the historical and theological links the Pentecostal movement has with the Holiness movement of the nineteenth century. Both areas must be localized in the context of Pentecostal worship, and essential to the ﬁeld of ethics are the affections and virtues, two moral frameworks that have proven useful for Christian moral reﬂection. Rather than choosing one or the other, Pentecostals can employ these frameworks in a complementary manner, for each framework has particular accents that are crucial for describing how the moral life takes shape and is sustained. The author employs the activity of ‘tarrying’ from Pentecostal worship as a metaphor for the Pentecostal vision of the moral life in order to show how Pentecostals may continue to embody distinctively their eschatological vision of God at a time when they are negotiating competing allegiances as they emerge as a sub-tradition within Christianity.

Annotated bibliography

Cross, Terry L. “The Divine-Human Encounter: Towards a Pentecostal Theology of Experience.” <i>Pneuma</i> 31, no. 1 (2009): 3–34. https://doi.org/10.1163/157007409X418121.

A programmatic lead article in <i>Pneuma</i> offering an account of experience as the divine–human encounter at the heart of Pentecostal theology. Vondey cites it for the claim that when the human ‘heart’ bears witness to the experience of God it is healed and ‘transformed into a dwelling place for Christ to live by the Spirit’. For the owner this is perhaps the key secondary source in the list: a Pentecostal theology of *encounter* as transformation, the exact term of the project, and a place to test whether ‘encounter’ needs patristic categories (indwelling, mingling, deification) to say what changes.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 192: Cited (n. 91) for the heart that bears witness to the experience of God being healed and transformed into a dwelling place for Christ by the Spirit.

Annotated bibliography

Calbreath, Donald F. “Serotonin and Spirit: Can There Be a Holistic Pentecostal Approach to Mental Illness?” In <i>Science and the Spirit: A Pentecostal Engagement with the Sciences</i>, edited by James K. A. Smith and Amos Yong, 133–52. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 2010.

A chapter in the first Pentecostal volume on theology and science, asking whether Pentecostal healing practice can hold biochemical accounts of mental illness (serotonin, medication) together with prayer and the Spirit. Vondey pairs it with Yong for the cure/healing distinction. For the owner it is a body–mind source (the later chapter on matter and spirit) and a caution against reading every encounter as a physical event.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 191: Cited (n. 83) with Yong for the distinction between curing a condition and healing the whole person.

Annotated bibliography

Yong, Amos. “Disability, the Human Condition, and the Spirit of the Eschatological Long Run: Toward a Pneumatological Theology of Disability.” <i>Journal of Religion, Disability & Health</i> 11, no. 1 (2007): 5–25. https://doi.org/10.1300/J095v11n01_02.

An article-length version of Yong’s pneumatological theology of disability, read in the light of the eschaton. Vondey cites it for the distinction between curing (restoring a body to a former state) and healing (the holistic transformation of a person to a new state of being), the very sentence the owner marked ‘A new type of person, beyond Adam. Deification here for sure’. Read this before building on that note: Yong’s point is partly that healing need not mean cure, which complicates any claim that bodily change is the sign of deification.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 191: Cited (n. 83) for healing as not a localized restoration of the body but the holistic transformation of a person to a new state of being.
  • p. 192–97: Also cited for kenotic healing (n. 89, p. 15), death followed by transition toward renewed existence (n. 103, p. 17) and eschatological embodiment (n. 117, pp. 17–21).

Annotated bibliography

Wenk, Matthias. “The Holy Spirit as Transforming Power within a Society: Pneumatological Spirituality and Its Political/Social Relevance for Western Europe.” <i>Journal of Pentecostal Theology</i> 11, no. 1 (2002): 130–42. https://doi.org/10.1177/096673690201100109.

A Swiss Pentecostal New Testament scholar (author of <i>Community-Forming Power</i> on the Spirit in Luke–Acts) argues that the Spirit’s transforming work is social and political, not only inward. Vondey cites it for the claim that the relational dimension of the Spirit’s transforming power ‘runs against much of Western individualistic, spiritualized and internalized ideas of the charismatic life’. It speaks to the owner’s ‘filled to be poured out’ note and is a Western European voice for the communal side of encounter.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 188: Cited (n. 71) for the relational dimension of the Spirit’s transforming power running against Western individualistic, internalized ideas of the charismatic life.

Annotated bibliography

Macchia, Frank D. “Baptized in the Spirit: Towards a Global Theology of Spirit Baptism.” In <i>The Spirit in the World: Emerging Pentecostal Theologies in Global Contexts</i>, edited by Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, 3–20. Grand Rapids, MI: Eerdmans, 2009.

Macchia’s shorter restatement of his Spirit-baptism thesis for a global volume edited by Kärkkäinen, examining the doctrine’s place in Pentecostal history and widening it toward a global theology. Vondey pairs it with Yong for Spirit baptism as an ‘intensification of the imago Dei’. A quick, citable summary of Macchia for the proposal, in a volume edited by one of the owner’s key Orthodox-dialogue voices.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 186: Cited (n. 62) with Yong for Spirit baptism as a point of encounter that sanctifies human nature and intensifies the image of God.

Annotated bibliography

Yong, Amos. <i>Spirit-Word-Community: Theological Hermeneutics in Trinitarian Perspective</i>. Eugene, OR: Wipf and Stock, 2002.

Yong’s trinitarian theological hermeneutics, in which knowing is shaped by Spirit (experience), Word (the given) and Community (interpretive tradition), built on a pneumatological ‘foundational’ metaphysics. Vondey cites pp. 160–61 for Spirit baptism as a point of encounter between the human spirit and the divine Spirit that sanctifies human nature and intensifies the imago Dei. For the owner it supplies a philosophical account of how encounter changes the person, which the patristic material lacks in modern terms.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 186: Cited (n. 62, pp. 160–61) for Spirit baptism as an encounter of human and divine spirit resulting in the sanctification of human nature and an ‘intensification of the imago Dei’.

Annotated bibliography

Macchia, Frank D. <i>Baptized in the Spirit: A Global Pentecostal Theology</i>. Grand Rapids, MI: Zondervan, 2006.

Macchia’s landmark proposal that Spirit baptism, widened beyond empowerment into a kingdom- and Trinity-shaped metaphor for the whole of salvation, is the organizing centre of Pentecostal theology. Vondey cites pp. 172–75 for Spirit baptism as ‘both an intensely personal and a communal experience’ that delivers the individual from isolation. It matters for the owner’s choice of Spirit baptism as the test case (findings §2b-2) and directly supports their margin note that Spirit baptism is ‘never an individual experience. We are filled to be poured out’.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 185: Cited (n. 53, p. 172; nn. 54–55, pp. 174–75) for Spirit baptism as both intensely personal and communal, delivering the individual from isolation for the transformation of self and others.

Annotated bibliography

Castelo, Daniel. <i>Revisioning Pentecostal Ethics: The Epicletic Community</i>. Cleveland, TN: CPT Press, 2012.

Castelo’s account of Pentecostal moral formation as the life of an ‘epicletic’ community, one that continually calls on the Spirit, with attention to the altar, the affections and practices that form virtue. Vondey cites it twice: for the affections in Pentecostal accounts of transformative encounter (pp. 35–38) and for the ‘holistic habits’ and ‘sanctifying practices… in communion with others’ that the altar requires (pp. 59–82). This is the most direct bridge in the chapter to the owner’s asceticism thread (findings §2b-12): encounter plus habit, epiclesis plus discipline. Castelo is also a supervisor candidate (findings §5).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 184: Cited (n. 45, pp. 35–38) for the role of the affections in Pentecostal accounts of spirituality and transformative encounter.
  • p. 184: Cited (n. 52, pp. 59–82) for the altar requiring holistic habits empowered by the Spirit and embodied in sanctifying practices in communion with others.

Annotated bibliography

Solivan, Samuel. <i>The Spirit, Pathos, and Liberation: Toward an Hispanic Pentecostal Theology</i>. Journal of Pentecostal Theology Supplement Series 14. Sheffield: Sheffield Academic Press, 1998.

A Hispanic Pentecostal theology built on ‘orthopathos’ (right feeling), set beside orthodoxy and orthopraxy, and on the Spirit’s transformation of suffering (pathos) into liberation. Vondey borrows its triad when he says the sanctification of the passions into right affections requires integration with right beliefs and right practices. For the owner, orthopathos is a ready term for how encounter reshapes the affections, and it sits close to the patristic healing of the passions (Palamas’s passions redirected, not killed, findings §2).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 184: Cited (n. 50, pp. 27–28) for the person transformed into the image of Christ only by embodying the image of the Spirit of Christ; n. 51 (Ibid., 60–69) supplies the orthopathos–orthodoxy–orthopraxy triad.

Annotated bibliography

Yong, Amos. “On Divine Presence and Divine Agency: Toward a Foundational Pneumatology.” <i>Asian Journal of Pentecostal Studies</i> 3, no. 2 (2000): 167–88.

An early methodological essay in which Yong engages Donald Gelpi’s ‘foundational pneumatology’ and argues for an account of the Spirit as divine presence and divine agency in the world, asking why Pentecostals and charismatics should care. Vondey cites it for the line that the pursuit of the image of Christ ‘is always an experience of the human spirit directed by and towards the Holy Spirit’. It is freely available online and is a good source for the owner on the Spirit’s *presence* (findings §3: the Spirit’s localized presence to the body).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 184: Cited (n. 49) for the pursuit of the image of Christ as always an experience of the human spirit directed by and towards the Holy Spirit.

Annotated bibliography

So, Tae Young. “Pentecostal Spirituality as Nurturing Vitality for Human Lives.” <i>Journal of Pentecostal Theology</i> 18, no. 2 (2009): 246–62. https://doi.org/10.1163/096673609X12469601162114.

A Korean Pentecostal essay on spirituality as the Spirit’s nurture of human vitality across the whole life of the person. Vondey cites it for the claim that human spirituality is a participation ‘in the effort to overcome the polychotomy of body, soul, and spirit, as well as of divine Spirit and human spirit’. For the owner it is a short way into an Asian Pentecostal account of whole-person transformation (body and soul together), near the language of synergy.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 183: Cited (n. 43) for human spirituality as participation in the effort to overcome the polychotomy of body, soul and spirit, and of divine and human spirit.

Annotated bibliography

Cross, Terry L. “The Yoke of Necessity: The Use of the Terms <i>Necessitas</i> and <i>Coactio</i> in the Thought of John Calvin.” In <i>The Spirit and the Mind: Essays in Informed Pentecostalism</i>, edited by Terry L. Cross and Emerson B. Powery, 157–77. Lanham, MD: University Press of America, 2000.

A Pentecostal theologian’s study of how Calvin distinguishes ‘necessity’ (the fallen will sins necessarily) from ‘coercion’ (it is not forced), in a Festschrift for Donald Bowdle of Lee University. Vondey cites it at the hinge of his argument: locating sin in human nature leads to ‘impersonalized deprivation and determinism’ with little room for perfection, while locating it in the person grounds ‘embodied responsibility for sanctification’. This is the one place in the chapter where Vondey names the Reformed alternative, so it is the source to read for the owner’s question of what makes Pentecostal participation different from evangelical/Reformed sanctification (and for the Torrance tension, findings §2b-7).

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 182: Cited (n. 37) for the contrast between locating sin in human nature (determinism, little room for perfection, i.e. Calvin) and in the person (embodied responsibility for sanctification).

Annotated bibliography

Yong, Amos. <i>Theology and Down Syndrome: Reimagining Disability in Late Modernity</i>. Waco, TX: Baylor University Press, 2007.

Yong’s major constructive work on disability, which rebuilds a pneumatological theological anthropology (the imago Dei, embodiment, healing and resurrection) from the experience of people with Down syndrome, including his brother. It argues against rational, functional and relational accounts of the image that exclude the intellectually disabled and for a relational, embodied, emergent view of the person. It is the single most-cited book in Vondey’s chapter (about a dozen notes), so it is effectively the chapter’s anthropological backbone. For the owner, it is a Pentecostal source on the body that is honest about healing that does not come and about impairment in the resurrection (Vondey p. 196) — a check on any account of encounter that only counts visible bodily change.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, “Humanity” (Pentecostal Theology, ch. 8):

  • p. 181: Cited (nn. 31–32, pp. 181–82) for the claim that not every human embodies the divine image in the same way: a difference in the quality of its embodiment, not in quantity.
  • p. 177–79: Also cited for the spiritual quality of the image (n. 7, pp. 169–70) and the Pentecostal critique of rational, functional and relational views of the imago Dei (nn. 12, 14, 15, 17).
  • p. 185–86: Cited for the image found in embodied, interdependent relations (nn. 56–57, pp. 180–81) and for Spirit baptism’s ontological effect (n. 63, pp. 181–91).
  • p. 192–97: Cited for healing versus cure (n. 86), the marks of impairment on the risen Jesus (n. 111, p. 175), and eschatological embodiment (nn. 116–17).

My writing: 2026-11-07 (Vondey, "Humanity"; proposal outline)

11.7.26 - Vondey and Anthropology

I semi-skinned a chapter in Vondery's book about anthropology, and it is right up the allye of where I am going. Pnls posit the Spirit transofmrs the whole person. Especailly telling is his use of Pentecost as a test case. The baptism in the Spirit is poured out on all flesh. This is an encompassing transformation. Along with this is also the physical encounter of healings and tongues. Grounded in the body, these Spirit encounter's are continually sanctifying the person both body and soul (and mind and emotions and whatever else you want to tag on here).

The human participation in santfication is indeed key here. Although, I wonder how novel this is in evangelical theolgoy anyway. Would anyones say you do not have to participate? What makes Pnl different? My hunch in Orthodoxy is that you actually increase, grow, our sprout wings and asenend. There is a very real ladder to climb, and so you better start climbing. Need more here. I know Karkannese has written on this a good bit between justification, santification, and deification. I may need to check them out.

Which brings me to the these. I need to being outlining it.

* Problem in the text (a problem that both in Pnl and Macarius address)

* Problem in the world (how this problem is experienced now)

* Good news in the text (Spirit baptism encounters through human participation create deification of the whole person)

* Good news in the world (How this good news affects us today)

So what is the Good News? The good news is that we are not stuck the way we are. There is a spiraling growth into Jesus. That we have Jesus here and now through the Holy Spirit, and not just know Him but He is continually transforming us with encounters of His presence. We are not alone.

The Good News at its core is that you can experience Jesus in a tangible way that creates lasting transformation.

In the text in Macarius, you see this often as the soul being taken over by Satan, but through prayer the Spirit encounters us and transforms us by giving us wings to be lifted up toward God.

In Pnl, in a similar way, through tarrying, the Spirit comes and transforms our whole person as we radiate more of the Image of God in the world (this is similar to what Kalistos Ware was talking about at baptism. There is a fulness of the Spirit that is hidden and can be made manifest more throughout deification)

It is like we have the image restored in a coin, but we continually shine the coin so the image becomes more clear (Joshua's words)

The Bad News. For Macarius, the Devil has taken over our souls. Full stop. That sounds pretty sucky. I wonder his demonology on this? Does the devil still have control post baptism, if so, how?

The bad news in Pnl? No sure.

I can imagine there being a thread of something in our human nature. Not ontologically, just experientially. We just don't want to. Really anything, it takes a big force of will to do most anything these days. Creating habits, caring for our kids. Especially, moving into seeking Jesus. It often feels like we are stuck and need to move through mud. At least, this is how I often feel.

Story in proposal: I was a charismatic pastor who tarried daily, setup a prayer house in our living room, called for healing each Sunday, for 2 and a half years. And we never felt a physical encounter with the Lord in our church. This felt like a failure. Burned out like bad toast, I sulked through my last week as a pastor. When someone came up to me, one of the back rowers types, who come every few Sundays. With tears in his eyes says, "You have no idea how much you and this church meant to us". His wife nodding her head vigorously. "There was something really special here."

I had missed the continual working of the Spirit, while waiting for the bug baptism.

Macarius in Wesley's writings (checked 2026-11-07)

# Macarius in John Wesley's own writings (checked 2026-11-07)

**Method:** full-text search for "Macari-" in (a) Curnock's *Journal*, Standard Edition, vols. 1–8 (London: Robert Culley, 1909–16; Internet Archive `a61369040[1-8]wesluoft`), and (b) *The Works of the Rev. John Wesley*, 3rd American ed., 7 vols. (New York, 1856; IA `worksofrevjohnwe0001wesl`, `worksofrevjohnwe0[2-7]wesluoft`). This covers the sermons, letters, treatises, prefaces and Journal; Wesley's private diaries (Bicentennial *Works* 18–19) and his letters in the Bicentennial edition were not searched. Ephrem Syrus is often named beside Macarius.

| # | Where (with the 1856 *Works* page) | Date | What Wesley says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Diary, 30 July 1736**, as summarized by Curnock, *Journal* 1:254 (n. 2: the Macarius extract "takes up 60 pp." in the *Christian Library*). The diary itself: Bicentennial *Works* 18:405–6 ("began Macarius" … "sang"; per Bundy 2004, not seen) | 1736 | "He read Macarius and sang" (three times that day, on a boat bound for Charleston) |
| 2 | **"An Extract from the Homilies of Macarius,"** *A Christian Library*, vol. 1 (Bristol: Felix Farley, 1749), 79–c. 155, with Wesley's introduction (pp. 79–c. 83) | 1749 | Wesley's own abridgment (22 homilies) |
| 3 | **Preface "To the Reader," *Christian Library* vol. 2** (to Foxe's *Acts and Monuments*), *Works* (1856) 7:528 area ("Abridgments of Various Works") | 1749 | "After the venerable remains of Ignatius and Polycarp, closed with the artless, yet lively, discourses of Macarius, and John Arndt's nervous account of true Christianity, worthy of the earliest ages …" |
| 4 | **Letter to the Rev. Dr Conyers Middleton** (1749), closing part (the "Plain Account of Genuine Christianity"), §11, *Works* (1856) 5:761 | 1749 | "All this may be allowed concerning the primitive Fathers; I mean particularly Clemens Romanus, Ignatius, Polycarp, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, Clemens Alexandrinus, Cyprian; to whom I would add Macarius and Ephraim Syrus." §12: "And yet I exceedingly reverence them … because they describe true, genuine Christianity." |
| 5 | **Sermon 43, "The Scripture Way of Salvation"** (1765), §I.7, *Works* (1856) 1:386 | 1765 | "How exactly did Macarius, fourteen hundred years ago, describe the present experience of the children of God! 'The unskilful, or unexperienced, when grace operates, presently imagine they have no more sin. Whereas they that have discretion cannot deny, that even we who have the grace of God may be molested again. … they were well nigh burned up.'" (The thought parallels Mason Hom. 50.4, p. 311, "the inexperienced man, being comforted by grace, imagines … that sin is rooted out"; the exact source homily is not pinned down.) |
| 6 | **Sermon "On Laying the Foundation of the New Chapel, near the City-Road"** (1777), §II.3, *Works* (1856) 1:492–93 | 1777 | The religion of love "is the religion of the primitive church … even in the fourth century, it was found in the works of Chrysostom, Basil, Ephrem Syrus, and Macarius." |
| 7 | **Editor's note (Henry Moore) on "Queries respecting the Methodists"** (Calvinistic controversy), *Works* (1856) 7:480–81 | — | Moore: "Mr. Wesley told me, that, at the time he wrote this, he believed, with Macarius, that all who are perfected in love … were thus elect. But he afterward doubted of this." (Moore, *Life of Mr. Wesley* 1:292) |

**Jackson (1872) equivalents** (the standard citation, not checked page by page): Sermon 43 = Jackson 6:43–54; New Chapel sermon = Sermon 112, Jackson 7:419–30; Letter to Middleton = Jackson 10:1–79.

**For the proposal:** #5 is the key text. Wesley uses Macarius as a witness to *present experience* in the very sermon that sets out his order of salvation (instantaneous and gradual sanctification). #4 and #6 rank him among the Fathers who show "true, genuine Christianity" and "the religion of love".

Heinz Berthold's critical Greek edition of Collection I of the Macarian corpus (the 64 logoi of Vaticanus graecus 694, 'B'), in two volumes (vol. 1: logoi 2–29; vol. 2: logoi 30–64), which Plested cites as 'I'. Your two new orange highlights are both Collection I passages on the vision of light: I 58.1.1–2.1, the 'perfect mystery of Christianity' as the soul's experience of 'the effulgence of the heavenly light ... in the revelation and power of the Spirit', and I 10.3.1–2, the saints who see 'with the unveiled face of the soul' how the glory is transformed 'from glory to glory' even while still in this world. Neither passage has a Collection II parallel in Edwards's concordance, so neither is in Mason; there is no English translation of Collection I (German: Fitschen 2000), so read them in Plested's and Edwards's translations. They matter for you because they make felt, luminous encounter 'the central and defining feature of the Christian life' (Plested) and set it in this life: the nearest Macarian ground for your 'Spirit baptism?' question. Already in your library (6IG7V6US, added from the Ware run today).

PDF p. 5–6 (print p. 128): Plested's proof text that the deifying vision of light is 'the central and defining feature of the Christian life': the 'perfect mystery of Christianity' is for every believing soul to receive the experience of the heavenly light in the power of the Spirit, not 'on the level of conceptual images' but as 'the true and hypostatic effulgence of the eternal light in the soul'; he then reads it through the Transfiguration (II 15.38).

PDF p. 6 (print p. 129): Plested's climax of the 'variety and complexity of the experience of deification' (on 2 Cor 3:18): those who bear the heavenly image of Christ, 'clad in the purple of the heavenly king (that is ... the heavenly joy of the Spirit)', see with the 'unveiled face' of the soul the glory transformed 'from glory to glory'; God does this 'even while they are in this world'.

Symeon's (949–1022) 225 short *Chapters* and three doctrinal discourses in English (144 pp.). Ware's orange n. 40 is Chapter 3.21, the climax of the paper: the person who has the light of the Spirit "falls prostrate… cries out and shouts", is "beside himself", and, washed by tears, "shines as lightning" until "God is joined in unity with gods". Ware says it has "obvious parallels in modern Pentecostalism". The same book gives n. 5 (1.35–36, the second baptism is "the truth itself") and n. 33 (3.76). For you, 3.21 is the strongest bodily-ecstatic text in the paper: falling, crying out, burning, tears and light, ending in deification. It belongs with your 'body and soul transformed in encounter' core and with the open gap "Symeon in the once-or-repeated debate" (findings §1, §3).

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "St. Symeon the New Theologian: 'he cries and shouts'" (PDF p. 13), n. 40 = Chapters 3.21: Ware's third answer for Symeon: the outward signs of the Spirit include prostration, shouting, fire and tears, with obvious Pentecostal parallels; Symeon's writings are popular among charismatic Orthodox.

data.note:
Annotated bibliography

Gregory of Nazianzus. *Festal Orations*. Translated by Nonna Verna Harrison. Popular Patristics Series 36. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2008.

Harrison's translation of Orations 1, 38, 39, 40, 41 and 45 (Easter, Nativity, Theophany, Baptism, Pentecost, Second Easter), with introduction and commentary. Ware's n. 40 says that the last phrase of Symeon's Chapter 3.21, "God is joined in unity with gods and is known by them", is Gregory's; it comes from *Or.* 38.7, repeated in *Or.* 45.3 (NPNF: God may "hold converse with us as Gods, being united to us"). So Symeon's ecstatic, bodily text ends on a Cappadocian deification formula. This is a direct line from your Cappadocians to Pentecostal-looking experience, through Symeon. The same volume holds *Or.* 40–41, already in your key passages (findings §2), so one book serves both.

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "St. Symeon the New Theologian" (PDF p. 13), n. 40: The phrase "God is joined in unity with gods and is known by them", with which Symeon crowns his description of ecstatic fire and tears, is identified by Ware as Gregory of Nazianzus's.

Annotated bibliography

John Climacus. *The Ladder of Divine Ascent*. Translated by Colm Luibheid and Norman Russell. Introduction by Kallistos Ware. Classics of Western Spirituality. New York: Paulist Press, 1982.

The thirty "steps" of the Sinai abbot's (c. 579–649) ascetic classic, read by Orthodox monks every Lent; this translation carries Ware's own introduction (and Norman Russell, of *Doctrine of Deification*, is co-translator). Ware takes two passages from it: obedience to a director as the sign that "the Holy Spirit has taken up residence in your soul" (Step 4), and the tears after baptism that are "greater than baptism itself" (Step 7). Your note on the first ("spiritual moms and dads… a helpful attendant to Pnls") makes this a source for a pastoral chapter on guided encounter. Step 7 on *penthos* answers the method warning in findings §4 (Grobnicu, Lysack): Pentecostals keep the experience and drop the tears and the ascesis. Note that Ware cites Migne (PG 88); this edition does not use the traditional verse numbering, so locate passages by step.

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "The worst of all heresies" (PDF p. 3): Named as the third test case, the author of *The Ladder*, "a work which Orthodox monks are supposed to reread each Lent".
  • p. "St. John Climacus: the baptism of tears" (PDF p. 10), nn. 27–28 (not marked orange): Step 4: being upbraided by your director yet loving him more is a sign of the Spirit's indwelling; Step 7: post-baptismal tears as a second baptism.

Annotated bibliography

Makarios/Symeon. *Reden und Briefe: Die Sammlung I des Vaticanus Graecus 694 (B)*. Edited by Heinz Berthold. 2 vols. Die Griechischen Christlichen Schriftsteller der ersten Jahrhunderte. Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1973.

The critical Greek edition of Collection I (Ware's "B"), the 64 logoi of Vaticanus graecus 694. Ware's orange n. 18 is here: B 43.6, where grace is at first so "subtle" that one is "unaware of its presence", but persistence in the virtues makes baptism "increase in power" and be "revealed in us". The same logos gives n. 15 ("Our baptism is true for us and valid"), and B 25.2 gives n. 19 ("one receives it with power and assurance, another with weaker energy"). These are exactly the two texts Edwards builds his "imperceptible grace becomes felt" argument on (I.43 at pp. 136–41, I.25 at pp. 141–44), and your calendar puts them on Sun Nov 29 (Edwards A). There is no English translation (German: Fitschen 2000), so read them in Edwards's translations.

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "The Macarian Homilies" (PDF p. 7), n. 18 = B 43.6: Ware's proof that Macarius, like Mark, moves from an unconscious baptismal gift to grace revealed "in power" through ascetic struggle.
  • p. "The Macarian Homilies" (PDF pp. 7–8), nn. 15, 19 = B 43.6, B 25.2 §§2–4 (not marked orange): Baptism the "source" of life in the Spirit; each person shares in baptismal grace "according to the measure of that person's faith and piety".

Annotated bibliography

Pseudo-Macaire. *Œuvres spirituelles*. Vol. 1, *Homélies propres à la Collection III*. Edited and translated by Vincent Desprez. Sources Chrétiennes 275. Paris: Éditions du Cerf, 1980.

The standard edition (Greek text with French translation, 399 pp.) of the homilies found only in Collection III (Ware's "C"); the first edition was Klostermann and Berthold, *Neue Homilien des Makarius/Symeon*, TU 72 (1961). Two of Ware's orange notes are here and not in Mason: C 28.3 (the "talent" of baptism, which can be lost if you do not work with it) and C 15.4 (the apostles who "cried out willy-nilly", like a flute that sounds as the player wants: Ware's possible allusion to tongues). No published English translation was found (Edwards, p. 11 n. 37, says Collection II is the only one in English), so for now Ware's and Edwards's own translations are the English. For you, C 15.4 is the one Macarian text that comes closest to glossolalia, and it is not in your Mason sessions.

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "The Macarian Homilies" (PDF p. 7), n. 16 = C 28.3: Baptism is complete ("you possess the talent in its completeness"), but unless you work with it you remain incomplete and "will be deprived of it". Ware notes that Mark would never say grace can be lost.
  • p. "The Macarian Homilies" (PDF p. 9), n. 25 = C 15.4: The Pentecost passage: "the Spirit spoke in them as He wanted", and in those who "resemble" the apostles. Ware calls it an "isolated passage" and warns against building on it.

Annotated bibliography

Mark the Monk. *Counsels on the Spiritual Life*. Translated by Tim Vivian and Augustine Casiday. Foreword by Rowan Williams. Popular Patristics Series 37. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 2009.

The complete works of Mark the Monk (the Hermit, the Ascetic; late 4th or early 5th century) in English, in two volumes bound as one: vol. 1 includes *On the Spiritual Law* and *Concerning Those Who Imagine That They Are Justified by Works*, vol. 2 *Concerning Holy Baptism* (Ware's "On Baptism"). Mark writes against the Messalians: baptism is complete, the Spirit is given "secretly" (*mystikōs*) at the font, and it becomes "active" (*energōs*), felt "with full assurance and sensation", only as we keep the commandments. Ware makes Mark the plumb line for the whole paper: the Spirit present but not yet felt, and "become what you are". For you he is the clearest patristic grammar for your own note that the Spirit is "there but hidden" in baptism and that participation is the key (PDF p. 5). He is also the anti-Messalian control against which Macarius is measured.

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "The worst of all heresies" (PDF p. 3): Named as the first of three esteemed writers (with Macarius and Climacus) against whom Ware tests whether Symeon is a "manic zealot" or typical of the East.
  • p. "St. Mark the Monk: from 'secret' to 'active' presence" (PDF pp. 4–6), nn. 8–14: Ware's main witness: baptismal grace is complete and given secretly; it is revealed actively through the commandments; Mark is reticent about visions and tears ("Do not grow conceited if you shed tears", n. 13).

Annotated bibliography

Lossky, Vladimir. *In the Image and Likeness of God*. Edited by John H. Erickson and Thomas E. Bird. Introduction by John Meyendorff. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1974.

A posthumous collection of Lossky's essays (232 pp.), the companion to *The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church* (already in your library, X35ZSD5T). It includes "Tradition and Traditions" (first published 1952 in *The Meaning of Icons*), where Tradition is "the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church": not a deposit of past formulas but the Spirit's present life. Ware uses that line in his opening to dissolve the stock contrast "Orthodoxy appeals to Holy Tradition, Pentecostalism to personal experience". For you it is the Orthodox warrant for saying that tradition and encounter are not rivals: a possible frame for your "confessional experience" method term (findings §2b-9). Pair it with Lossky's chapter on the economy of the Spirit in *Mystical Theology*.

How it is used in Kallistos Ware, "Personal Experience of the Holy Spirit according to the Greek Fathers" (1997):

  • p. "Solovetsk and Sunderland" (PDF p. 2), n. 2: Ware quotes Lossky's definition of Holy Tradition as "the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church" here and now, to argue that no one can be a Christian "at second-hand" and that Orthodoxy is not merely tradition against Pentecostal experience.

Annotated bibliography (from Ware 1997)

Your reading text for Macarius (Collection II, Ware's "H"), already in your library and the spine of sessions A–F. Ware's Collection II citations land on it directly: the trance and the man "like a fool or a barbarian to this world" (H 8.3, Mason p. 66, session C), the naked soul that must "weep and beseech the Lord" for the Spirit's garment (H 20.1, p. 163), the "unseemly outcries" at prayer (H 6.4, p. 58), and the four "baptism of fire and the Spirit" texts (H 26.23, 27.17, 32.4, 47.1). These are the same four Edwards treats as sacramental (pp. 89–96). Ware reads them as the conscious, higher stage of baptismal grace, which gives you a second, Orthodox reading to set against Edwards.

"The worst of all heresies" (PDF p. 3): Named as the second test case: the Homilies "attributed to St. Macarius of Egypt, but in fact of Syriac origin (late fourth century)".

"The Macarian Homilies: light, tears and ecstasy" (PDF p. 8), n. 23 = H 20.1 (Mason p. 163): Tears as the way to the Spirit's power: whoever is "naked" of the Spirit's garment should "weep and beseech the Lord".

"The Macarian Homilies" (PDF p. 9), n. 24 = H 8.3 (Mason p. 66): The ecstatic case: a man "swallowed up in the sweetness of contemplation" is no longer master of himself. This is Ware's evidence that Macarius, unlike Mark, describes trance and ecstasy.

"The Macarian Homilies" (PDF pp. 8–9), nn. 20–22, 26 (not marked orange): "Baptism with fire and the Spirit" as the higher conscious stage (H 26.23, 27.17, 32.4, 47.1), light (H 1–8, 10), fire (25.9–10) and the warning against "unseemly cries" (H 6.3–4).

data.annotationText: All agree that the ‘second baptism’ – the baptism of tears or ‘baptism with the Holy Spirit’ is an extension and fulfilment of the first baptism bestowed sacramentally with water. ‘Spirit baptism’ is not to be seen as conferring an entirely new grace, different from that conferred through ‘water baptism’.

person who has within him the light of the most Holy Spirit, unable to endure it, falls prostrate upon the ground; and he cries out and shouts in terror and great fear, for he sees and experiences something that surpasses nature, thought and imagination. He becomes as one whose entrails have been set ablaze: devoured by fire and unable to bear the scorching flame, he is beside himself, and he cannot control himself at all. And though he sheds unceasing tears that bring him some relief, the fire of his longing is kindled to yet fiercer flames. Then he weeps more abundantly and, washed by the flood of his tears, he shines as lightning with an- ever-increasing brilliance. When he is entirely aflame and becomes as light, then is fulfilled the saying, ‘God is joined in unity with gods and is known by them. 40
First of all, he lays great emphasis upon the gift of tears: the second baptism is precisely ‘a baptism of tears

When Symeon speaks of Baptism in the Spirit, he means the grace of the renewal of sacramental Baptism. It is the same grace of the Spirit that makes water-Baptism a sacrament, which in turn makes possible the gradual renewal of the image…. The grace man receives in Baptism, which promotes his spiritual growth, acts as a starting-point in which the end is present in the beginning. 39

Through divine baptism we become children and heirs of God, we are clothed with God Himself, we become His limbs, and we receive the Holy Spirit who comes to dwell within us, which is the royal seal…. All these things, and other things yet greater than these, are given to the baptized immediately from the moment of divine baptism. 38
Let no one say, ‘ I have received and I possess Christ from the moment of holy baptism.’ Such a person should recognize that it is not all the baptized that’receive Christ throu

Symeon – more than Mark the Monk, more even than the Macarian Homilies – attaches crucial importance to the attainment, by every Christian without exception, of a direct, conscious awareness of the Spirit; and this may sometimes lead him to exaggerated statements.
Do not say that one can possess Him without knowing it.’30 Taken literally, these words suggest that Symeon identifies the reality of grace with the conscious awareness of it.
Not only will he be saved, but he will receive help – at first, without being aware of it, then with conscious awareness, and soon afterwards with the illumination that comes from Almighty God. 3

To some contemporary Christians there might seem to be a contradiction between, on the one hand, strict obedience to a spiritual guide and, on the other, the personal experience of freedom in the Holy Spirit. But this is not the way in which Orthodoxy views the matter. On the contrary, it is precisely through obedience that we learn freedom. The role of the spiritual guide or ’soul friend’ (Celtic amchara) is not to act as a substitute for the Spirit, but it is specifically through our relationship with our guide that we are helped to attain personal awareness of the Spirit’s presence. So far from discouraging a direct contact with the Spirit, our guide seeks to open the door for us; to vary the metaphor, he or she aims to be transparent.
data.annotationComment: This is huge as well, the idea of spiritual moms and dads in the faith. Sometimes we have mentors but this could be a helpful attendant to Pnls, the Orthodox view of having a spiritual guide

There are some who during prayer make use of unseemly cries, as if relying on their own bodily strength, not realizing how their thoughts deceive them, and thinking that they can achieve perfect success by their own strength. 26
data.annotationComment: Is this not charismatic prayer? I have seen this countless times. If you have to say this in a church, then you are actively experiencing these things.

data.annotationText: But this is an isolated passage which has no exact parallel elsewhere in Macarian corpus, and so it would be unwise to base too much upon it.
the degree to which someone shares in this grace depends on the measure of that person’s faith and piety. 19
data.annotationComment: The other side of the deification coin. One side is that we participate, the other is that if we don’t, then grace seems to be lacking.

data.annotationText: But if we persist and advance in all the virtues, struggling with full exertion, then baptism will increase in power and will be revealed in us, making us perfect through its own grac
This, as we have noted, is exactly Mark’s teaching: through our fulfilment of the commandments and our ascetic struggles, the hidden grace of baptism is gradually ‘revealed’ in its full pow

Just as Mark envisages a progress from baptismal grace present ’secretly’ to baptismal grace experienced ‘actively’, so likewise the Homilies maintain that the indwelling presence of the Spirit, conferred at baptism, is something of which we ere initially unconscious

The Homilies concur with Mark in insisting furthermore upon the completeness of baptism: ‘In possessing the pledge of baptism, you possess the talent in its completeness, but if you fail to work with it, you yourself will remain incomplete; and not only that, but you will be deprived of it.’ 16
data.annotationComment: Participation

data.annotationText: In agreement with Mark, the Macarian Homilies see sacramental baptism as the foundation of all Christian life: ‘Our baptism is true for us and valid, and it is the source from which we receive the life of the Spirit.’ 15

St. Augustine, Pascal or John Wesley. Personal experience of the Spirit permeates their whole life, existing as a total awareness, without necessarily being crystallized in the form of particular ‘experiences’.

When interpreting an author such as Mark, it is helpful to make a distinction between ‘experience’ (in the singular) and ‘experiences’ (in the plural). There are surely many Christians who feel able to say in all humility, ‘I know God personally’, without being able to point to any single event such as a vision, a voice, or a concentrated ‘conversion crisis’ of the kind undergone by St. Paul,
data.annotationComment: That is key as well. The energies in experiences instead of one marking moment. While I have many experiences, I cannot point to one experience. This can be helpful for someone who has never felt God, and yet knows He is present.

data.annotationText: As to the outward experiences which accompany this conscious awareness of the indwelling Spirit, Mark is reticent. He does not speak about visions, dreams, trances and ecstasy.
Everything is contained implicitly in the initial charisma of baptism.

At the same time Mark regards this ‘secret’ presence as no more than an initial starting-point; and he clearly affirms that the vocation of every baptised Christian without exception is to advance from this to a conscious awareness of the Spirit.

While we cannot ‘add* to the completeness of baptism, God nevertheless awaits a response on our part; and if we fail to make that response, although the Spirit will still continue to be present ‘secretly’ in our heart, we shall not feel His presence ‘actively’ within us, nor experience His fruits with full conscious awarenes
data.annotationComment: Participation is KEY again here. I like this version of HS in baptism, there but hidden.

data.annotationText: Our spiritual programme can therefore be summed up in the maxim ‘Become what you are’.

indwelling presence of the Holy Spirit is given to us ‘secretly’, in such a way that we are not at first consciously aware of it. We only become ‘actively’ conscious of this presence if we acquire a living faith, expressed through our practice of the divine commandments.

Christ, being perfect God, has bestowed upon the baptized the perfect grace of the Spirit. We for our part cannot possibly add to that grace, but it is revealed and manifests itself increasingly, the more we fulfil the commandments …. Whatever, then, we offer to Christ after our regeneration was already hidden within us and came originally from Him.

Let us display, then, an apophatic reticence in all that we assert concerning the free and sovereign Spirit, who is like the wind that ‘blows where it chooses: and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know where it comes from or where goes’ (John 3:8).
data.annotationComment: This and the above paragraph are reticent of how Pnls devirbe Spirit theology, we can know some but the Spirit is the Spirit, which is why we promote experience over theology.

Annotated bibliography (from Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation ch. 11)

Rybarczyk, Edmund J. Beyond Salvation: Eastern Orthodoxy and Classical Pentecostalism on Becoming Like Christ. Paternoster Theological Monographs. Carlisle: Paternoster, 2004.

The standard Pentecostal–Orthodox comparative monograph: theosis and classical Pentecostal sanctification set side by side on the shared aim of becoming like Christ, covering anthropology, means of grace (liturgy and ascesis vs revival, altar and personal piety) and the vision of transformation. Kärkkäinen cites it in n. 286, without a page, as his evidence that 'significant similarities have been recently uncovered between Orthodox and Pentecostal pursuits of holiness', noting Pentecostalism's Holiness roots. This is now the second reading to send the owner to Rybarczyk for the Orthodox–Pentecostal link on holiness (Vondey cited it twice at p. 77). It is already in the library and in Encounter Research, and is on the calendar for Nov 20–21 (final comparative chapter).

p. EC p. 271 (PDF p. 26); n. 286 on EC p. 286 (PDF p. 41): Cited as the recent study showing that Orthodox and Pentecostal pursuits of holiness are alike, a link Kärkkäinen grounds in Pentecostalism's nineteenth-century Holiness roots and Wesley's reading of the Eastern Fathers.

Annotated bibliography

Lossky, Vladimir. The Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church. Translated by members of the Fellowship of St. Alban and St. Sergius. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1976. First published London: James Clarke, 1957.

The classic twentieth-century Orthodox synthesis (French original 1944), which shaped how Western readers see theosis: apophatic theology, the essence–energies distinction, and the separate 'economy' of the Holy Spirit. Kärkkäinen's n. 57 points to pp. 196–99, which (as far as we know, unchecked) open ch. 10, 'The Way of Union'. That chapter treats union with God as synergy, the free cooperation of human will with grace, and Kärkkäinen also cites ch. 10 for union in n. 36. He uses it for the line the owner marked purple: grace is 'a presence of God within us that demands constant effort on our part'. For the owner, this is the Orthodox text behind Kärkkäinen's synergy, and the place to test his own pursuit/tarrying thread (findings §2b-7) against an Orthodox account of effort inside grace. Findings §2 already notes that Lossky's Spirit chapter is ch. 8.

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC pp. 250–51 (PDF pp. 5–6); n. 57 on EC p. 280 (PDF p. 35): Supports the claim that in the East grace and freedom are never set against each other: 'It is not a question of merit but of cooperation, a synergy. Grace is a presence of God within us that demands constant effort on our part.'
  • p. EC p. 249 (PDF p. 4); nn. 36, 41 (also n. 56, p. 174): Cited elsewhere in the same section for union with God (ch. 10) and for theosis being 'echoed by the fathers and the theologians of every age'.

Annotated bibliography

Peacocke, Arthur. Theology for a Scientific Age: Being and Becoming—Natural, Divine, and Human. Enl. ed. Theology and the Sciences. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1993.

Peacocke's Gifford Lectures, the major statement by the biochemist-priest of a theology fitted to an evolving cosmos (God as continuous creator acting in and through natural processes; panentheism). In the same orange highlight as Polkinghorne, Kärkkäinen cites p. 430 n. 22, where Peacocke says deification is probably 'more congenial to an evolutionary perspective than the traditional, often Western, language of redemption, salvation, sanctification, etc.' The page number points to the enlarged 1993 edition (the 1990 Blackwell first edition is far shorter). For the owner this is a second science-and-theology voice to pair with Polkinghorne in a later Spirit-and-matter chapter: on this view theosis is the frame that suits a world of growth and becoming. Peacocke is a liberal panentheist, so he is a conversation partner, not an ally on bodily encounter.

How it is used in Veli-Matti Kärkkäinen, Spirit and Salvation, ch. 11 "One with God":

  • p. EC p. 275 (PDF p. 30); n. 325 on EC p. 288 (PDF p. 43): A second 'scientist-priest' supporting the claim that deification language suits an evolutionary, creation-wide account of salvation better than Western forensic terms.

Annotated bibliography

Polkinghorne, John. Reason and Reality: The Relationship between Science and Theology. London: SPCK, 1991.

A short (119-page) book by the Cambridge mathematical physicist turned Anglican priest, setting out his 'critical realism' and arguing that science and theology are both truth-seeking disciplines about one reality. Kärkkäinen's n. 324 cites p. 103, where (as Kärkkäinen reports it) Polkinghorne grants that the Orthodox may be right that deification is 'the destiny of creation'. That fits Polkinghorne's wider eschatology: creation is destined to share in God's life, and the new creation is what the Spirit does with the old one, not a replacement. For the owner it is a lead for the later body–matter chapter: deification read as the Spirit's transformation of matter, not only of souls. Same-year US edition: Philadelphia: Trinity Press International, 1991 (ISBN 1-56338-019-6). Which edition Kärkkäinen used is not stated in the chapter.

Also, one thing i think is missing in this is asceticism on the road to deification. I want to learn more about this both in Macarius, thhe fathers, orthodoxy, and how it differes from asceticism in medieval west when we think about that. Fasting and all night prayer is a huge part of Pnl, I know several people who have been on 40 day fasts, almost unheard of in other traditions!

My writing: 2026-11-05 (Macarius Hom. 1, 12, 18, 30, 32, 47; and Kärkkäinen)

11.5.26 - Macarius and Karkaenin Alright, I have read a lot and written little. I do not want this toi seep out of my mind, so I want to capture some of it.

First, I really love reading Macarius. Like that dude gets it. He writes in an emobodied way that enlivens the pruist of Jesus throuhg the Spirit. It is not systematic, and it has no dry elements. It is a lived writing as Macarius seems to be writing to people right in front of him.

And that dude is honest. Describing a monk who would pray in his cell together and had seen healing in his life, falling into sin later and leaving Jesus. Man, the amount of Pnls who can understand being late at night in a prayer room tarrying for the Spirit, encountering him in power, and then oen of them falling into drugs or sex later.

Too many stories to count.

He talks about lived encounters with the Spirit - inexpressible joy and laughter, weeping in tears for the salvation of humanity, healings, and baptism in the Spirit with fire. This dude was pentecostal before Pentecostals.

He seems to be relatively unwritten in Pnl circles, which seems like something that needs to be written about. Especailly from a pastoral heart, seeing the drive of Macarius to share his real life of the SPirit with others, it feels like he is wtiting in a way, contemporary charistmatics could actually understand.

A couple key elements from him. First is the encounter piece. Obviously huge and helpful. Especially when it onyl felt like a couple lines in Tertullian and a few in other patristics is all the Pnl type experieences we get. Whereaas, Macarius has several moments of talking about the radical encouters with the Spirit.

Second, there is a real pursuit of Jesus that is at home in Pnls. A very real tarrying, waiting, seeking of Jesus. In fact that is what we are here to do, to seek the Lord. And to keep seeking him when it gets difficult. He even in a recent homily I read will pull back His presence in order to strengthen us to seek Him ore. He often talks about seeking and pursuing Jesus until He comes! Or at least until the grace is given. Is that not Jeremy's Riddles famous song, "Come Lord Jesus, Come!"

In the same manner there is a participation with the Spirit, a mingling as Macarius calls it. That the Spirit enlivens our Spirits to do good works and to fight he battle against the enemy. I like the participation language.

Dr. Marcus Plested calls Macarius the greatst patristic on deification, and that is true. Deification is all throughout his writings. I like his apt metaphor that the Spirit gives us wings to ascend to God. That is beautiful. Although, we do not become God and are not lost in Him (like Evagarius mentions). We contain our hypostasis and dwell within God as we are carried up to Him.

Really it comes down to tarrying on the pursuit to be more like Jesus as we are defied through the Holy SPirit. This is what tracks with Pnl and what I want to study. That we tarry, He encounters, we are filled and pour out. That process is Pnl to its core.

Then I read a chapter of Karkaneean talking about jsutification by faith alone and eastern Orthodox theosis. He mentioned the desperate need for us tpo learn from the Orthodox on one key issue, becoming more holy. That this is a journey with Jesus as we grow in holiness. Not something we are given at the moment of faith. Pnls especially the ideas of strugglign with the Lord to be more like Him.

Definitely something here.

I want to look at Vondey again on encounteres and expoerience.

While he remains hidden as to essence God gives and reveals himself to his creatures raising them up through his processions powers and energies to theosis to union and assimilation with him as far as is possib

Moses is “neither himself nor another” as he is united not to the essence but to the deifying activity of God. Human individuation in other words remains even as humans are deied. For Dionysius Moses remains Moses and we might presume to add Peter remains Peter and Paul remains Paul. The unions may prevail over the distinctions but the distinction nonetheless endures.

This is of course precisely the ecstasy experienced by Moses when he enters into the divine darkness of Sinai and “being neither himself nor another is through an inactivity of all knowledge united in his highest part with the wholly unknowable and by knowing nothing knows in a manner that transcends mind” (MT 1.3).

Macarius lays down a profoundly Trinitarian account of deication that is both Spirit-led and Christ-centered bringing human beings to the throne of the Fathe

Does some form of epektasis (unceasing progress) give way to something more like rest or repose? While one can assume a certain indefectibility after death—one is not going to lapse back into sin in heaven—Macarius like all the best theologians is content with a certain level of paradox and uses paradigms of both rest and movement to characterize theosis on both sides of the veil (with the emphasis perhaps on movement in via and on rest in patria). The nal line of the last-quoted passage neatly encapsulates this enduring double character of deication: in heaven the children of light both repose in light and shine out ever and anew in that same light.

Annotated bibliography (from Plested, Oxford Handbook ch. 8)

Pseudo-Macarius. Fifty Spiritual Homilies of St. Macarius the Egyptian. Translated by A. J. Mason. Translations of Christian Literature, Series I: Greek Texts. London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1921.

Mason's 1921 English translation of Collection II of the Macarian corpus (the Fifty Spiritual Homilies), the collection Plested calls 'the most widespread' and cites as 'II'. Plested himself cites the critical Greek edition, Hermann Dörries, Erich Klostermann and Matthias Kroeger, eds., Die 50 geistlichen Homilien des Makarios, Patristische Texte und Studien 4 (Berlin: de Gruyter, 1964); Mason's homily and section numbers match it, so every 'II n.n' reference can be read here. The two passages the owner flagged are the places where Macarius uses the technical verb ἀποθεόω ('is deified'), which Plested calls 'striking and somewhat novel' as a standard term for the believer's deification. Both set deification inside spiritual struggle and Spirit-wrought rebirth, and both say the deified person goes beyond Adam: the core of the owner's question of encounter as real transformation. Already in the owner's library and in the Macarius reading plan (sessions D and F).

p. PDF p. 4 (print p. 126): Plested quotes the answer to the question whether natural desire is eradicated with sin when the Holy Spirit comes (a question-and-answer section of Hom. 26, on the soul's worth and its temptation by Satan): man by the Spirit and spiritual rebirth not only reaches the first Adam's measure but 'is made greater than him, for man is deified (ἀποθεοῦται)', as his first example of Macarius spelling out deification in technical terms.

p. PDF p. 4 (print p. 126): Plested's second example of ἀποθεόω: the 'good spiritual warrior' who subdues his own soul comes to good measures of the Spirit, 'is made greater than himself; for such a one is deified (ἀποθεοῦται), and made a son of God, receiving the heavenly stamp upon his soul'.

Annotated bibliography

Vondey, Wolfgang. “The Theology of the Altar and Pentecostal Sacramentality.” In <i>Scripting Pentecost: A Study of Pentecostals, Worship and Liturgy</i>, edited by Mark J. Cartledge and A. J. Swoboda, 94–107. Explorations in Practical, Pastoral and Empirical Theology. Routledge, 2016.

Vondey’s own chapter (ch. 6 of the volume) on the altar as the centre of Pentecostal worship and on a Pentecostal account of sacramentality built from it. In “Religion as Play” he uses it for the claim that the altar service is “the summit and source” of Pentecostal worship, into which other practices and their doctrines are gathered as “altar call and response”. It is the bridge between this article and <i>Pentecostal Theology: Living the Full Gospel</i> (2017), where the altar becomes the organising metaphor of the whole system (the owner has read pp. 74–122). For the owner’s project, encounter at the altar as transformation of body and soul, it is the shortest statement of how Vondey ties altar, sacrament and encounter together, and it puts the Pentecostal altar in conversation with sacramental (including Orthodox) traditions.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 10: Cited (Vondey 2016), with Tomberlin 2010, for the altar call and response as “the climax of traditional Pentecostal worship.”
  • p. 10: Cited (Vondey 2016, pp. 99–106) for the altar service as “the summit and source of Pentecostal worship, rituals, and practices”, with other practices and their doctrinal reflections integrated into the central ritual of altar call and response, the ground of an “altar hermeneutics”.

Some details unverified, see sources.json.

Annotated bibliography

Tomberlin, Daniel. <i>Pentecostal Sacraments: Encountering God at the Altar</i>. Cleveland, TN: Center for Pentecostal Leadership and Care, 2010.

A Church of God (Cleveland, TN) pastor-theologian’s case that Pentecostal worship is sacramental: preferring “sacrament” to “ordinance”, Tomberlin presents water baptism, the Lord’s Supper and foot washing (with anointing and the laying on of hands) as means of grace in which believers encounter the Holy Spirit, and treats the altar as the centre and focus of Pentecostal worship. It is an updated edition of his 2006 study <i>Encountering God at the Altar: The Sacraments in Pentecostal Worship</i>, written partly as practical guidance for pastors. Vondey pairs it with his own chapter for the claim that the altar call and response is the climax of Pentecostal worship. For the owner it is the most direct Pentecostal treatment of encounter at the altar as something that happens through material, bodily means, and a natural bridge to Orthodox sacramental and deification language.

How it is used in Wolfgang Vondey, Religion as Play:

  • p. 10: Cited with Vondey 2016 for the claim that, among Pentecostal rituals, “the altar call and response stand out as the climax of traditional Pentecostal worship.”

Annotated bibliography (from Russell, ch. 7)

Basil of Caesarea. "De Spiritu Sancto (On the Holy Spirit)." Translated by Blomfield Jackson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd ser., vol. 8. Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing, 1895. New Advent: Church Fathers. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3203.htm.

Basil's mature treatise (c. 375) on the Holy Spirit's equal glory with the Father and Son, written for Amphilochius of Iconium. Chapter 9.23 is the most famous deification text in Basil: through the Spirit souls are purified, become 'spirit-bearing' and radiant like transparent bodies struck by a sunbeam, pass their grace on to others, and reach 'the highest goal of all, becoming a god'. Russell reads it as social, eschatological and Spirit-centred rather than simply Plotinian. This is already in the owner's library (Jackson's NPNF translation, the one Russell uses); for a modern version see Stephen M. Hildebrand's translation, On the Holy Spirit (Popular Patristics 42, SVS Press, 2011, ISBN 978-0-88141-876-7). For the owner it is the core Cappadocian text for Spirit-encounter as transformation, purification of the passions, and a deification that overflows to others.

p. 209: De Sp. S. 9.23 (PG 32.109BC) is quoted at length (trans. Jackson, modified) as the most famous reference to human divine destiny in Basil; Russell notes its social character and argues, against Henry's Plotinian reading, for a Christian background (Hippolytus, Methodius, Clement).

p. 211: De Sp. S. 9.23 (PG 32.109AB): the Spirit makes human beings spiritual, conforms them to the image of the Son and raises them to the archetypal beauty, with first fruits in baptism and fulfilment only in heaven.

p. 211: De Sp. S. 1.2 (PG 32.69B): after glorifying God, the Christian aim is likeness to God as far as human nature allows; the telos is the blessed life of the age to come.
